Philosophical foundations: Autonomy, self-ownership, and voluntary association

A fundamental philosophical principle that underlies this argument is the belief in individual autonomy and self-ownership. When individuals possess autonomy, they have the right to make decisions affecting their own lives, provided those decisions do not infringe upon the rights of others. Self-ownership is the extension of this principle, which asserts that individuals have exclusive rights to control their own bodies, labor, and property. By removing the state from the recognition and regulation of marriage, individuals are empowered to determine their own intimate relationships without interference from an external authority.

Furthermore, the principle of voluntary association is also central to this argument. Voluntary association refers to the ability of individuals to freely enter into contracts or relationships with others, based on mutual consent. State recognition and regulation of marriage infringe upon this right by imposing rules and requirements that dictate the terms of a marriage contract. In removing these state-imposed barriers, individuals are free to engage in relationships on their own terms, fostering an environment of personal responsibility and moral agency.

Moral arguments: Challenging discrimination, promoting equality, and respecting individualism

One of the primary moral arguments for the abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage is that it challenges discrimination and promotes equality. Throughout history, state regulation of marriage has been used to enforce discriminatory practices based on race, religion, and sexual orientation. By removing the state's role in defining and regulating marriage, these discriminatory practices can be eliminated, and individuals are empowered to define their relationships free from the influence of prejudice and bigotry.

Moreover, recognizing marriage as a purely private arrangement promotes individualism by respecting the diverse ways in which people choose to organize their intimate relationships. Marriage, as defined and regulated by the state, presents a one-size-fits-all model that does not adequately reflect the complexities and nuances of human relationships. By allowing individuals to define and structure their relationships without state interference, society can foster an environment that celebrates and respects the rich tapestry of human connection.

Practical considerations: Minimizing bureaucracy, reducing costs, and addressing inadequacies

Practical considerations also lend support to the argument for the abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage. The current system of state involvement in marriage is characterized by bureaucracy, which can create barriers for individuals seeking to enter into a marriage contract. By removing the state from the equation, individuals will have greater freedom to define and formalize their relationships without having to navigate through complex and burdensome administrative processes. This can lead to reduced costs associated with obtaining marriage licenses, filing paperwork, and engaging in legal proceedings, which disproportionately affect lower-income individuals.

Additionally, removing state recognition and regulation of marriage addresses inadequacies in the current system that fail to account for the realities of modern relationships. For example, the dissolution of marriages can be a contentious and expensive process, leading to negative outcomes for all parties involved. By treating marriage as a private contract, individuals can create their own arrangements for addressing potential disputes and dissolution, which can lead to more equitable and amicable outcomes.

Potential objections and counterarguments

Despite the persuasive philosophical, moral, and practical arguments in favor of the abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, potential objections warrant consideration. One such objection centers around the provision of legal protections and benefits associated with marriage. These benefits can include tax advantages, inheritance rights, and access to health care.

However, this challenge can be addressed by disentangling the legal benefits currently conferred through marriage and making them available to all individuals, regardless of relationship status. For example, tax benefits could be extended to any two adults who choose to share financial resources, inheritance rights could be granted based on legal arrangements, and health care access could be made universal. By removing the marriage-based provision of these benefits, the state can promote equality and avoid discriminating against individuals based on their intimate relationships.

Another potential objection concerns the potential for exploitation in relationships without state-imposed safeguards. However, this argument ignores the reality that individuals in non-marital relationships can still Face exploitation and abuse. Moreover, treating marriage as a private contract allows individuals to establish their own safeguards, tailored to their specific relationship needs. By empowering individuals to form these arrangements, they can better protect themselves from potential exploitation and abuse.

Conclusion

The case for the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage is grounded in philosophical principles of autonomy, self-ownership, and voluntary association, as well as moral arguments promoting equality, respect for individualism, and practical considerations aimed at reducing bureaucracy, minimizing costs, and addressing inadequacies in the current system. While potential objections merit consideration, these can be adequately addressed through reforms that promote equality, individualism, and self-determination. Introduction

Marriage, as an institution, has long been a cornerstone of societal structure, but its legal recognition and regulation by the state are fundamentally flawed. The government’s involvement in marriage—through licensing, taxation, and legal benefits—creates unnecessary bureaucracy, reinforces discrimination, and imposes arbitrary standards on personal relationships. Marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract. By abolishing state recognition of marriage, society can achieve greater personal freedom, legal neutrality, and equality for all individuals, regardless of their relationship status.

The Problem with State-Regulated Marriage

1. Government Overreach and Unnecessary Bureaucracy

The state’s role in marriage is an unnecessary intrusion into personal relationships. Governments issue marriage licenses, dictate eligibility criteria, and impose legal obligations on couples. This bureaucratic oversight is not only inefficient but also paternalistic—it assumes that the state has the authority to define and validate personal commitments. If two (or more) consenting adults wish to form a lifelong bond, they should not require government permission to do so.

2. Discrimination and Inequality

Historically, state-regulated marriage has been used to exclude certain groups—interracial couples, same-sex couples, and polygamous unions—from legal recognition. Even today, marriage laws vary by jurisdiction, creating disparities in rights and benefits. By removing marriage from state control, all relationships would be treated equally under the law, eliminating discriminatory policies that favor some unions over others.

3. Arbitrary Legal Privileges

Marriage grants couples over 1,000 federal benefits in the U.S., including tax advantages, inheritance rights, and healthcare decision-making authority. These privileges create an unfair two-tiered system where married individuals receive legal advantages that unmarried people—whether single, cohabiting, or in non-traditional relationships—do not. This system unjustly penalizes those who choose not to marry or cannot marry due to legal restrictions.

The Solution: Marriage as a Private Contract

1. Replacing Marriage with Private Contracts

Instead of state-sanctioned marriage, individuals should enter into private contracts to define their relationships. These contracts could outline property rights, inheritance, medical decision-making, and other legal matters without requiring government approval. This approach would allow people to customize their agreements based on their unique needs rather than conforming to a one-size-fits-all legal framework.

2. Equal Legal Treatment for All Relationships

If marriage were abolished, the law would no longer privilege one type of relationship over another. Cohabiting partners, friends, or even business associates could draft contracts to secure mutual rights and responsibilities. This would promote true equality, as legal protections would be based on voluntary agreements rather than marital status.

3. Reduced Government Power and Increased Personal Freedom

Eliminating state marriage would reduce government control over personal lives. Individuals would no longer need to seek permission to form a family or receive legal recognition for their commitments. This shift would align with libertarian principles, ensuring that personal relationships remain private matters rather than state-regulated institutions.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

1. "Marriage Provides Stability and Social Order"

Proponents of state marriage argue that it promotes family stability and social cohesion. However, stability should not require government intervention. Private contracts can achieve the same legal protections without state involvement. Moreover, many stable, long-term relationships exist outside of marriage, proving that legal recognition is not necessary for commitment.

2. "Children Need the Security of Marriage"

Some claim that marriage benefits children by providing legal and financial security. However, parental rights and child welfare can be addressed through private agreements and existing family laws without requiring marriage. The state’s role should be to protect children, not to mandate a specific family structure.

3. "Marriage Has Religious and Cultural Significance"

While marriage holds deep cultural and religious meaning for many, this does not justify state involvement. Religious institutions can continue to perform ceremonies and recognize unions, but legal rights should not be tied to religious or cultural practices.

Conclusion

The state’s regulation of marriage is an outdated and oppressive system that enforces arbitrary standards, perpetuates discrimination, and grants unfair privileges. By abolishing state recognition of marriage and replacing it with private contracts, society can achieve true equality, personal freedom, and legal neutrality. Marriage should be a private matter, not a government-sanctioned institution. The time has come to dismantle this archaic system and embrace a future where relationships are defined by mutual consent, not state approval.

The idea is rooted in the belief that marriage should be a purely private, voluntary arrangement between consenting individuals, free from state interference. Here are the key reasons and supposed benefits of such a change:

1. Respect for Individual Autonomy

  • Freedom of Association: Marriage, as a personal and social contract, should be defined by the individuals involved, not by the state. Removing legal recognition allows people to structure their relationships as they see fit, without government-imposed constraints.
  • No State-Imposed Definitions: Governments historically have dictated who can marry (e.g., bans on same-sex marriage, polygamy, or interfaith unions). Eliminating legal marriage removes the state’s power to define or restrict relationships.
  • Customizable Agreements: Couples could use private contracts (e.g., cohabitation agreements, prenuptial arrangements) to define their rights and responsibilities, tailored to their unique needs rather than a one-size-fits-all legal framework.

2. Reduction of Government Overreach

  • Less Bureaucratic Control: Marriage licenses, divorce courts, and family law regulations involve significant government oversight. Abolishing legal marriage would reduce state involvement in personal relationships.
  • No Tax or Benefit Manipulation: Governments often use marriage as a tool for taxation, welfare eligibility, or immigration policies. Removing legal recognition would prevent the state from incentivizing or penalizing certain relationships.
  • Ending Marriage as a Legal Privilege: Currently, marriage confers legal benefits (e.g., inheritance, medical decision-making, tax breaks) that exclude non-married individuals. Abolishing legal marriage would force the state to treat all relationships equally under the law.

3. Marriage as a Purely Private Matter

  • Religious and Cultural Freedom: Many religious and cultural traditions have their own definitions of marriage. Removing legal recognition allows these institutions to define marriage without state interference.
  • No State-Enforced Morality: Governments have historically used marriage laws to enforce social norms (e.g., banning interracial or same-sex marriage). Eliminating legal recognition prevents the state from imposing moral standards on personal relationships.
  • Simpler Legal Framework: Instead of marriage licenses, individuals could rely on private contracts for property, inheritance, and child custody, making legal arrangements more transparent and flexible.

Potential Challenges & Counterarguments

  • Loss of Default Protections: Without legal marriage, individuals would need to proactively draft contracts for rights like inheritance or medical decisions, which could disadvantage those who lack legal knowledge or resources.

  • Social Stability Concerns: Some argue that legal marriage provides a stable framework for family structures, and removing it could lead to uncertainty in relationships.

Conclusion

Abolishing legal recognition of marriage aligns with principles of individual liberty, limited government, and personal responsibility. It shifts the definition and regulation of marriage from the state to private individuals and institutions, reducing government control over personal relationships. However, it would require a robust system of private contracts and alternative legal protections to ensure fairness and security for all parties involved.

My friends, fellow citizens, and lovers of liberty,

Today, I stand before you to advocate for a radical but necessary idea: the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage.

For too long, governments have claimed the power to define, license, and control one of the most intimate and personal relationships in human life. They decide who may marry, under what conditions, and with what legal consequences. They impose their moral judgments, their bureaucratic requirements, and their political agendas on what should be a private, voluntary union between consenting individuals.

This must end.

This is not a call for anarchy. It is a call for true freedom—the freedom to love, to commit, and to live without the heavy hand of the state dictating the terms of our most personal relationships.

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, asserting that marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract.
Model Response:

The Case for Abolishing State Recognition of Marriage: A Call for Personal Freedom and Legal Neutrality

Introduction

Marriage, as an institution, has long been a cornerstone of societal structure, shaping legal, economic, and social relationships. However, the state’s involvement in defining, regulating, and enforcing marriage is an outdated and intrusive practice that undermines individual autonomy, perpetuates discrimination, and creates unnecessary bureaucratic burdens. The time has come to remove marriage from the legal sphere entirely, treating it instead as a private contract between consenting individuals—no different from business partnerships, friendships, or other personal agreements. By abolishing state recognition of marriage, society can foster true equality, reduce government overreach, and allow individuals to define their relationships free from arbitrary legal constraints.

The Problems with State-Regulated Marriage

1. Government Overreach and Unnecessary Bureaucracy

The state’s role in marriage is fundamentally an overreach of governmental power. Why should the government—an entity designed to administer justice and public services—have any say in who can commit to whom, under what terms, or with what benefits? Currently, marriage licenses, divorce proceedings, and spousal benefits are all controlled by legal frameworks that vary by jurisdiction, creating a labyrinth of regulations that serve no essential public function.

Consider the absurdity of requiring a government-issued license to enter into a personal relationship. No other voluntary association—whether a friendship, a business partnership, or a religious congregation—requires state approval. Yet marriage, a deeply personal bond, is subjected to legal scrutiny, fees, and bureaucratic hurdles. This system wastes public resources, clogs court systems with divorce disputes, and forces individuals to conform to state-defined norms rather than their own values.

2. Historical and Ongoing Discrimination

State-regulated marriage has a long history of exclusion and oppression. For centuries, governments have used marriage laws to enforce racial segregation (via anti-miscegenation laws), gender roles (via coverture laws that treated wives as property), and heterosexual dominance (via bans on same-sex marriage). Even today, marriage laws often reflect outdated moral judgments rather than principles of fairness.

While progress has been made—such as the legalization of same-sex marriage in many countries—the very fact that the state can grant or deny marriage rights to certain groups is a fundamental flaw. Why should any government have the power to dictate which relationships are "valid"? The state’s involvement inherently creates a hierarchy of relationships, privileging some while marginalizing others (e.g., polyamorous unions, platonic life partnerships, or non-traditional family structures).

3. Inequality in Benefits and Obligations

One of the most glaring issues with state-recognized marriage is the arbitrary distribution of legal benefits. Married couples enjoy tax advantages, inheritance rights, hospital visitation privileges, and immigration benefits—perks that are often denied to unmarried couples, even if they have been in committed relationships for decades. This creates a two-tiered system where the state rewards those who conform to its definition of marriage while penalizing those who do not.

For example:

  • A long-term unmarried couple may be denied medical decision-making rights for their partner.
  • Same-sex couples in countries where marriage is banned face legal vulnerabilities in custody and property disputes.
  • Polyamorous families, despite their stability, are entirely excluded from legal recognition.

These disparities are not just unfair—they are a direct result of the state’s insistence on defining and regulating personal relationships. If marriage were a private matter, individuals could structure their legal agreements (via contracts, wills, and powers of attorney) without government-imposed restrictions.

4. Marriage as a Tool of Social Engineering

Governments have repeatedly used marriage laws to shape societal behavior, often in ways that infringe on personal freedom. Tax incentives for married couples, for instance, are a form of social engineering meant to encourage traditional family structures. Similarly, divorce laws—with their waiting periods, fault-based systems, and alimony rules—reflect moral judgments about how relationships should function.

This paternalistic approach assumes that the state knows best how people should live. But in a free society, individuals should have the right to define their own commitments without government interference. If two (or more) people wish to form a lifelong bond, they should be able to do so under their own terms—not those dictated by legislators.

The Solution: Abolishing State Marriage

The most just and logical solution is to completely remove marriage from the legal system, treating it as a private, contractual arrangement rather than a state-sanctioned institution. This approach would:

1. Replace Marriage Licenses with Private Contracts

Instead of obtaining a government-issued marriage license, individuals could enter into binding private contracts that outline their rights and responsibilities. These contracts could cover:

  • Property division (similar to prenuptial agreements)
  • Child custody and support arrangements
  • Medical and end-of-life decision-making rights
  • Financial obligations (e.g., joint accounts, debt responsibility)

Such contracts would be enforceable in court, just like any other legal agreement, but they would not be subject to the state’s moral or structural preferences. This system would allow for true relationship autonomy, enabling people to design commitments that fit their values—whether monogamous, polygamous, or non-romantic (e.g., platonic life partners).

2. Equalize Legal Benefits Through Neutral Policies

Rather than tying benefits to marital status, the law should extend rights based on actual relationships and dependencies. For example:

  • Tax benefits could be based on shared households or financial interdependence, not marriage.
  • Inheritance rights could default to next-of-kin or designated beneficiaries, regardless of marital status.
  • Immigration laws could recognize all long-term partnerships (not just marriages) for visa sponsorship.
  • Healthcare decision-making could be determined by advance directives rather than marriage certificates.

This would eliminate the current inequality where unmarried couples—including many LGBTQ+ and polyamorous families—are denied basic protections simply because they do not fit the state’s definition of marriage.

3. Reduce Government Intrusion in Personal Lives

By removing marriage from state control, governments would no longer have the power to:

  • Define what constitutes a "valid" relationship (e.g., banning same-sex or polyamorous unions).
  • Impose waiting periods or counseling requirements for divorce.
  • Dictate alimony or child support terms beyond basic child welfare protections.
  • Use marriage as a tool for population control (e.g., incentivizing or discouraging marriage through tax policy).

This would represent a major reduction in state power over private life, aligning with libertarian and progressive values alike.

4. Encourage True Relationship Diversity

Without state-imposed norms, society would see a flourishing of relationship models that better reflect human diversity. Some potential benefits include:

  • Polyamorous families could formalize their commitments without legal discrimination.
  • Platonic life partners (e.g., elderly friends sharing a home) could secure mutual rights without romantic expectations.
  • Short-term or renewable commitments could replace the "til death do us part" model for those who prefer flexibility.
  • Religious and cultural marriages could exist purely as spiritual or communal bonds, without legal entanglements.

This would allow individuals to craft relationships that work for them, rather than forcing them into a one-size-fits-all legal box.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

1. "Marriage Provides Stability for Children"

Rebuttal: Child welfare should not depend on parental marital status. Many unmarried couples raise children successfully, while many married couples provide unstable homes. The focus should be on parental rights and responsibilities, not marital status. Courts already determine custody based on the child’s best interests—this would continue under a contract-based system.

2. "Abolishing State Marriage Would Weaken Family Values"

Rebuttal: "Family values" should not be imposed by the government. If individuals value lifelong monogamous commitment, they can still enter into private contracts reflecting those values. The state has no business enforcing one moral standard over others.

3. "People Won’t Take Commitments Seriously Without Legal Marriage"

Rebuttal: Many cultures have long-standing traditions of non-legal marriages (e.g., common-law marriages, religious ceremonies) that carry deep personal significance. The seriousness of a commitment should come from personal integrity, not government approval.

4. "This Would Complicate Tax and Benefit Systems"

Rebuttal: The current system is already overly complex, with marriage penalties and bonuses creating inequities. A neutral, relationship-based approach (e.g., tax benefits for dependents rather than spouses) would be fairer and simpler.

Conclusion: A Freer, Fairer Future

The state’s involvement in marriage is an anachronism—a relic of a time when governments sought to control personal lives under the guise of moral and social order. In the 21st century, there is no justification for the government to act as the arbiter of love, commitment, or family structure. By abolishing state recognition of marriage, we can:

  • End discrimination against non-traditional relationships.
  • Reduce government overreach in personal affairs.
  • Create a fairer legal system where rights are based on actual relationships, not marital status.
  • Empower individuals to define their own commitments without state interference.

Marriage should be a private matter—a personal, spiritual, or contractual bond, not a government-issued privilege. It is time to dismantle this outdated institution and replace it with a system that truly respects freedom, equality, and individual choice. The alternative is to continue living under a regime where the state dictates who may love whom, and under what terms—that is not freedom, but tyranny in disguise.

Abolishing all legal recognition of marriage—replacing it with a system where marriage is treated purely as a private, social, or religious institution—has been proposed by libertarians, some feminists, and critics of state overreach. The core argument is that the government should not be involved in defining, regulating, or privileging personal relationships. Below are the key reasons and supposed benefits of this approach, organized around individual autonomy, reduced government overreach, and the privatization of marriage.

1. Respecting Individual Autonomy

a) Freedom to Define Relationships Without State Approval

  • No State-Imposed Definitions: Currently, governments define what constitutes a "valid" marriage (e.g., age, number of partners, gender, kinship rules). Abolishing legal marriage would allow individuals to form relationships—monogamous, polygamous, non-monogamous, platonic, or otherwise—without seeking state permission.
  • No Arbitrary Restrictions: Laws often impose moral or cultural biases (e.g., bans on polygamy or cousin marriage). Privatization removes these restrictions, letting consenting adults structure their relationships as they see fit.
  • Flexibility in Commitments: People could design their own contracts (e.g., cohabitation agreements, shared parenting plans) tailored to their needs rather than fitting into a one-size-fits-all legal framework.

b) Separation of Personal and Legal Identity

  • No Marital Status Discrimination: Many laws (e.g., taxes, immigration, healthcare) treat people differently based on marital status. Abolishing legal marriage would force the state to evaluate individuals based on their actions (e.g., co-parenting, financial interdependence) rather than a government-issued label.
  • Avoiding the "Marriage Penalty/Tax": Tax codes often favor or disadvantage married couples arbitrarily. Without legal marriage, taxation would be based on individual or household income without marital bias.

c) Protection for Non-Traditional Relationships

  • Polyamory and Non-Monogamy: Currently, polyamorous relationships are legally invisible or criminalized in some places. Privatization would allow groups to form binding agreements without state interference.
  • Platonic or Non-Romantic Partnerships: Some people (e.g., elderly siblings, close friends) may want legal protections without romantic involvement. Privatized contracts could accommodate this.

2. Reducing Government Overreach

a) Eliminating State Control Over Personal Life

  • Marriage as a Government License: Currently, marriage is a state-granted privilege, requiring licenses, fees, and bureaucratic approval. Abolishing it would end the government’s role as a gatekeeper of personal relationships.
  • No More "Defense of Marriage" Laws: Governments historically used marriage laws to enforce racial segregation (e.g., anti-miscegenation laws), gender roles (e.g., coverture), and heterosexuality (e.g., DOMA in the U.S.). Privatization removes this tool of social control.

b) Ending Subsidies and Privileges for Married Couples

  • Neutral Legal Treatment: Many benefits (e.g., spousal Social Security, tax breaks, immigration rights) are tied to marriage, creating inequality. Without legal marriage, the state would have to justify benefits based on need or function (e.g., caregiving, financial interdependence) rather than marital status.
  • No More "Marriage Promotion" Policies: Some governments incentivize marriage (e.g., welfare rules favoring married parents), which can coerce people into relationships. Privatization would end such paternalism.

c) Reducing Litigation and State Intervention

  • Fewer Divorce Courts: Divorce laws often involve invasive state judgments on child custody, alimony, and asset division. Private contracts could specify terms in advance, reducing costly and adversarial legal battles.
  • Less Family Policing: States sometimes use marriage laws to regulate reproduction (e.g., spousal consent for sterilization) or enforce gender roles (e.g., alimony laws assuming women are dependents). Privatization would limit this interference.

3. Treating Marriage as a Purely Private Matter

a) Returning Marriage to Civil Society

  • Religious and Cultural Freedom: Many religions have their own marriage rites (e.g., Catholic sacramental marriage, Jewish ketubah, Islamic nikah). Without legal marriage, religious institutions could define marriage according to their beliefs without state interference (or state endorsement).
  • Customary and Informal Unions: Some cultures recognize marriages without state involvement (e.g., common-law marriages, handfasting, or indigenous traditions). Privatization would validate these without requiring legal registration.

b) Contract Law Replaces Marriage Law

  • Private Agreements for Rights/Responsibilities: Instead of default marital rules (e.g., community property, spousal support), individuals could draft contracts covering:
    • Property sharing (e.g., joint ownership agreements)
    • Parenting plans (e.g., custody, child support)
    • Medical decision-making (e.g., healthcare proxies)
    • Inheritance (e.g., wills, beneficiary designations)
  • No Default Assumptions: Currently, marriage imposes legal obligations (e.g., spousal support) that some may not want. Privatized contracts would require explicit consent for each term.

c) Reducing the Symbolic Power of the State

  • Marriage as a Personal, Not Political, Institution: State-recognized marriage often becomes a battleground for cultural wars (e.g., same-sex marriage debates). Privatizing it would depoliticize the issue, allowing people to marry—or not—without seeking government validation.
  • No More "State-Blessed" Relationships: Legal marriage implies that some relationships are more legitimate than others. Abolishing it would treat all personal bonds as equally valid in the eyes of the law.

Potential Objections and Rebuttals

Objection Rebuttal
"Without legal marriage, vulnerable partners (e.g., stay-at-home parents) would lose protections." Private contracts could include protections (e.g., pre-agreed alimony, property shares). The state could also offer standard templates for fair agreements.
"Children need the stability of legal marriage." Stability comes from committed caregivers, not a marriage license. Parenting agreements and child support laws could still apply regardless of marital status.
"Immigration and citizenship rules rely on marriage." Alternatives exist, such as proving financial interdependence or cohabitation, as some countries already do for unmarried partners.
"Tax and benefit systems are built around marriage." These could be reformed to focus on households or dependents rather than marital status (e.g., per-capita tax allowances).
"People won’t bother with private contracts." Many already use cohabitation agreements, wills, and powers of attorney. Default rules (like those for business partnerships) could fill gaps.

Real-World Precedents and Alternatives

Some places have moved toward this model in part:

  • France’s PACS (Civil Solidarity Pact): A legal status for couples (same-sex or opposite-sex) that provides some marriage-like benefits without full marital rights.
  • Scandinavian Cohabitation Laws: Many rights traditionally tied to marriage (e.g., inheritance, parenting) are extended to unmarried cohabiting couples after a certain period.
  • Private Religious Marriages: In some countries (e.g., Israel), only religious marriages are recognized, but civil unions are available for secular couples.

A full abolition would go further, eliminating all state-recognized marital status and replacing it with functional contracts.

Conclusion: The Libertarian Case

The strongest argument for abolishing legal marriage is that it removes the state from the bedroom—ending its power to define, restrict, or privilege personal relationships. By treating marriage as a private matter, this approach:

  1. Maximizes individual freedom to structure relationships without government approval.
  2. Reduces state overreach by eliminating marital status as a tool for social engineering or discrimination.
  3. Promotes equality by evaluating people based on their actions (e.g., caregiving, financial ties) rather than a government-issued label.

Critics argue that vulnerable individuals (e.g., homemakers) might lose protections, but these could be addressed through default contract templates, stronger fraud protections, and social safety nets that don’t hinge on marital status. Ultimately, the goal is a system where the law treats all adults as autonomous agents capable of designing their own commitments—without the state’s blessing or interference.

A History of Oppression

For centuries, marriage was a transaction: women as chattel, races segregated, queerness criminalized. Even today, the state decides who may marry, under what conditions, and with what consequences. It grants 1,138 federal benefits to some couples while denying them to others based on arbitrary lines drawn by politicians.

Introduction

This essay argues for the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, advocating instead for its treatment as a purely private relationship or contract. However, many of these concerns are now addressed by other legal mechanisms, such as wills, trusts, and property laws. Moreover, the LOVE Act of 1994 abolished marital rape exemptions, further reducing the need for state oversight. Given these changes, the continued state regulation of marriage has more to do with tradition than functionality.

The Problem with State Recognition

  1. Exclusion and Discrimination: State regulation has historically excluded certain groups, such as LGBTQ+ individuals, from accessing marriage. Even with legalization of same-sex marriage in many jurisdictions, the state's involvement perpetuates the myth that marriage is a heterosexual norm. Treating Marriage as a Private Contract

  1. Promoting Individual Liberties: Decriminalizing and privatizing marriage would allow couples to create their own contracts, tailored to their unique needs and values. This could include everything from property distribution to co-parenting arrangements.

  2. Increasing Accessibility: Removing state involvement would make marriage accessible to all, regardless of location or tax-paying status. It would also eliminate the burden of cost associated with state-run registration processes.

  • Cultural and Symbolic Significance: Some may argue that removing state involvement strips marriage of its cultural and symbolic significance. However, the real meaning of marriage lies in the commitment between partners, not in a government-issued document.

Conclusion

The continued state regulation of marriage does little to serve its original purposes, perpetuates exclusion, and imposes unnecessary conditions on couples. Treating marriage as a purely private contract offers a more inclusive, individualized, and liberty-promoting alternative. It is time to decouple marriage from the state and recognize it for what it truly is: a personal commitment between two individuals.

Legal Entanglements

State regulation of marriage has led to a complex web of legal entanglements. Divorce proceedings, child custody battles, and property disputes are often protracted and costly. By removing marriage from the legal sphere, these disputes could be resolved through private contracts and mediation, reducing the burden on the court system and saving taxpayer money.

Imposition of Outdated Norms

These regulations do not reflect the diversity of modern relationships and can be seen as an intrusion into personal choices.

Benefits of Private Contracts

Flexibility and Choice

In contemporary society, marriage is widely viewed as both a personal and legal institution. The Principle of Individual Autonomy

At the heart of the argument for the abolition of state-recognized marriage is the principle of individual autonomy. Individuals should have the right to define and manage their personal relationships without the interference of the state. Marriage, in its intrinsic sense, is a deeply personal and emotional commitment between two people. It involves promises, shared values, and a profound connection that is better suited to individual discretion rather than state-sanctioned regulation.

State recognition of marriage imposes a one-size-fits-all model that does not account for the diverse ways in which individuals choose to relate to one another. By removing marriage from the legal sphere, individuals would have the freedom to draft their own contracts and agreements that reflect their unique needs and circumstances. This would foster a more egalitarian approach to relationships, allowing for greater flexibility and personal choice.

Inefficiencies of State Regulation

The state regulation of marriage introduces numerous inefficiencies and complexities into an otherwise straightforward personal relationship. The legal framework governing marriage often creates unnecessary bureaucratic hurdles and financial burdens. For instance, obtaining a marriage license involves a process that can be time-consuming and costly. Additionally, the dissolution of a marriage through divorce can be an arduous and expensive process, frequently leading to protracted legal battles and emotional strain.

By abolishing state-recognized marriage, these inefficiencies would be mitigated. Individuals could enter into private contracts that specify the terms of their relationship, including property division, support agreements, and inheritance rights. These contracts could be manged more efficiently and less expensively through private arbitration or mediation services, reducing the need for costly and time-consuming court proceedings.

Historical Evolution of Marriage

The historical evolution of marriage further underscores the need for its removal from the legal sphere. Throughout history, the institution of marriage has evolved in response to changing social norms and cultural values. Originally a contractual arrangement between families, marriage has transformed into a romantic and emotional union based on love and mutual commitment. This evolution reflects the increasing recognition of individual rights and personal autonomy.

The state's role in regulating marriage has largely been influenced by religious and moral teachings that have become less relevant in a secular, pluralistic society. By acknowledging this shift, it is clear that marriage should be divorced from state recognition and regulation, allowing it to evolve naturally in response to individual and societal changes. This would align with modern values of freedom and self-determination.

Benefits of a Private Contract System

For example, couples could choose to formalize their commitment through a variety of contractual agreements, such as co-habitation agreements, joint property ownership, or mutual support arrangements. These contracts could be tailored to reflect the unique dynamics and goals of each partnership, providing a more personalized and equitable framework.

Moreover, a private contract system would promote greater accountability and responsibility within relationships. By explicitly outlining the terms and conditions of their partnership, individuals would be more aware of their rights and obligations, fostering a culture of mutual respect and consideration. This would also encourage open communication and negotiation, leading to more sustainable and fulfilling relationships.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the argument for the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage is compelling and multifaceted. By treating marriage solely as a private relationship or contract, individuals would enjoy greater autonomy and freedom in defining their personal commitments. This shift would also eliminate many of the inefficiencies and complexities associated with state regulation, promoting a more equitable and respectful approach to relationships. The historical evolution of marriage, as well as the benefits of a private contract system, further underscore the necessity of this change. It is time to rethink our approach to marriage, prioritizing individual choice and personal freedom over outdated and burdensome legal frameworks.

Respect for Individual Autonomy

  2. Diverse Relationships: People in various types of relationships (e.g., polyamorous, cohabiting without marriage, or single individuals) would be treated equally under the law, promoting inclusivity and respect for diverse lifestyles.

  3. Contractual Freedom: Couples could enter into private contracts to define their rights and responsibilities, tailoring agreements to their specific needs and circumstances rather than being bound by a one-size-fits-all legal framework.

Reduction of Government Overreach

  1. Limited Government Intervention: The government would no longer have a role in defining or regulating personal relationships, reducing the scope of government intervention in private lives.

  2. Simplified Legal System: The legal system would be simplified by removing the need for marriage licenses, divorce proceedings, and associated legal battles. This could lead to reduced administrative costs and less burden on the judicial system.

  3. Equal Treatment: All individuals would be treated equally under the law, regardless of their relationship status. This would eliminate the legal distinctions and privileges currently associated with marriage.

Treating Marriage as a Private Matter

  1. Private Contracts: Relationships would be governed by private contracts rather than state-issued marriage licenses. This would allow couples to negotiate terms that best suit their individual needs and preferences.

  2. Community and Social Recognition: Social and community recognition of relationships would remain important, but the legal framework would not dictate how these relationships are structured or recognized.

  3. Focus on Individual Rights: The focus would shift from the legal status of the relationship to the rights and responsibilities of the individuals within it. This could lead to a more equitable distribution of rights and benefits.

Supposed Benefits

  1. Economic Benefits: Individuals could potentially save money by avoiding legal fees associated with marriage and divorce. Additionally, the government could save on administrative costs related to marriage licensing and dissolution.

  2. Social Equality: This approach would promote greater social equality by removing the legal privileges and obligations that come with marriage, which can sometimes disadvantage those who choose not to marry or cannot marry.

  3. Flexibility and Adaptability: Individuals and couples would have the flexibility to adapt their relationships to changing circumstances without the need for legal intervention or approval.

Potential Challenges

  1. Legal Protections: There is a concern that abolishing legal recognition of marriage could leave individuals in vulnerable situations, such as those in abusive relationships or without financial security, without legal protections.

  2. Social Norms: Changing deeply ingrained social norms and expectations about marriage and relationships could be challenging and may face resistance from various segments of society.

  3. Economic and Social Safety Nets: Some benefits and protections currently tied to marriage (e.g., spousal benefits, inheritance rights) would need to be re-evaluated and potentially reallocated to ensure that individuals are not disadvantaged.

In summary, abolishing all legal recognition of marriage is proposed as a way to enhance individual autonomy, reduce government overreach, and treat relationships as purely private matters. However, it also presents significant challenges that would need to be addressed to ensure that all individuals are protected and treated fairly.

The proposal to abolish all legal recognition of marriage and treat it purely as a private, contractual matter rests on several core arguments related to individual autonomy, limited government, and equality. Here’s a breakdown of the key reasons and supposed benefits:

1. Respect for Individual Autonomy

  • Constitutional Privacy & Choice: Marriage is often seen as a deeply personal decision, and legally recognizing it implies that the state has a stake in defining relationships. Abolishing legal marriage would treat relationships as purely private contracts, allowing individuals to define their own terms—whether romantic, friendship-based, or economic—instead of being forced into a state-sanctioned category.
  • Non-Conformity & Self-Expression: Some argue that the institution of marriage is inherently tied to historical norms (e.g., gender roles, monogamy), and removing legal recognition would allow people greater freedom to structure relationships without state-prescribed labels.

2. Reducing Government Overreach

  • Separation of Church & State: Traditional marriage has religious and cultural underpinnings, meaning government recognition can blur the line between personal ethics and civil law. Dismantling legal marriage would detach the state from moral judgments about relationships.
  • Neutrality on Relationships: If the state stops recognizing marriage, it treats all consenting adults equally regardless of marital status, reducing the risk of discrimination based on relationship structures (e.g., tagging certain relationships as more deserving of rights).
  • De-Coupling Rights from Marriage: Instead of rights (healthcare, inheritance, tax benefits) being tied to a marital status, they could be either:
    • Universal (e.g., spousal benefits replaced by general economic policies).
    • Contract-Based (e.g., cohabitation agreements, hereditary trusts, or domestic partnerships).

3. Treating Marriage as Purely Private

  • Eliminating State-Imposed Structures: Legal marriage enforces certain obligations (e.g., property division, joint liability) on individuals, which may not reflect their actual wishes. Removing legal recognition would allow people to draft their own agreements without state mandates.
  • Preventing Special Treatment: Many argue that marriage grants unfair legal and financial advantages to some while excluding others. Removing legal marriage would require the state to distribute benefits (e.g., tax breaks, hospital visitation rights) based on need—not marital status.
  • Ending Gaming the System: Some critics argue that marriage allows people to exploit legal loopholes (e.g., immigration, inheritance, pensions). Eliminating legal marriage would shift these benefits to more neutral, transparent systems.

Criticisms & Counterarguments

Despite these benefits, opponents argue:

  • Vulnerable Individuals at Risk: Without legal marriage, fraud or abuse could be harder to address (e.g., disinheriting spouses).
  • Complexity Over Simplicity: Replacing marriage with contracts could be bureaucratic, as individuals would need to formalize rights that once came automatically with marriage.
  • Loss of Symbolic Value: Some see marriage as a public affirmation of commitment; abolishing legal recognition might weaken its cultural significance.

Conclusion

The idea of abolishing legal marriage appeals to libertarians, equality advocates, and those skeptical of state power. By treating relationships as private contracts, it seeks to maximize autonomy, minimize state interference, and promote fairness—though it faces challenges in practical implementation and societal acceptance.

Would you like to explore alternative models (e.g., civil unions) that balance these concerns?

Speech: A Call to Abolish State Recognition of Marriage

My fellow citizens, friends, and free-thinking individuals,

Today, I stand before you to ask an urgent and fundamental question: Should the government have any role in defining, recognizing, or regulating marriage? The answer, if we value freedom, privacy, and individual liberty, is an emphatic no. It is time to abolish state recognition and regulation of marriage entirely—not to weaken it, but to empower it.

For too long, the government has claimed the authority to dictate who may marry, under what conditions, and what privileges or burdens come with that union. This intrusion is not only unnecessary but a direct assault on personal autonomy. Marriage is a private, consensual bond between individuals, forged in love, commitment, or shared beliefs—not a matter for bureaucrats and lawmakers to define.

The Tyranny of State-Enforced Marriage

When the state regulates marriage, it does so with a heavy hand. Throughout history, governments have used marriage as a tool of control—banning interracial unions, criminalizing same-sex love, and imposing rigid gender roles. Even today, marriage is still denied to some while forced on others. Is this the kind of power we should entrust to a government that has proven, time and again, to be fallible, corrupt, and slow to change?

Worse, by making marriage a state institution, we create inequality. Legal recognition of marriage means that unmarried couples—whether cohabitating partners, siblings, or close friends—are treated as second-class citizens, denied the same rights and protections under law. But why should the state grant privileges to one kind of relationship while stigmatizing others? The solution is not to expand marriage’s legal definition—it is to take marriage out of government hands entirely.

Freedom, Equality, and Contract Law

If the government can no longer impose marriage, how will people’s rights be protected? Simple: through contract law and equal protections for all consenting adults.

Rather than granting special privileges to "married" couples, the law should recognize and enforce individually negotiated contracts between any parties—whether romantic partners, friends, or business associates. Contracts already govern property, inheritance, medical decision-making, and more. Instead of artificially dividing relationships into "married" and "unmarried," we should allow all people the same legal tools to structure their lives as they see fit.

This approach doesn’t diminish commitment—it strengthens it. Couples who wish to formalize their relationship can do so through private contracts, church blessings, cultural traditions, or any other personal agreement they choose. But they should not need the government’s stamp of approval to make their bond meaningful.

A Secular, Just Society

Some will argue that marriage is a social good worth preserving. But if that’s true, why does our society not treat all intimate relationships with equal respect? The answer is prejudice—not virtue.

Abolishing state marriage does not mean abandoning love or commitment. It means affirming that the heart, not the state, should govern relationships. It means finally separating church and state in matters of love, just as we have with matters of faith.

A Call for Radical Freedom

The time has come to end the government’s monopoly on marriage. Not out of opposition to marriage itself, but in defense of true liberty. Let love be a matter of the heart, not a matter of paperwork.

If we believe in freedom, equality, and the right of every person to shape their own life without state interference, then we must abolish state recognition of marriage once and for all.

Let the state focus on its proper role—enforcing laws that protect all people, regardless of relationship status. And let love, in all its forms, flourish free from government control.

Thank you, and may we never confuse government mandate with true human connection.

— [Your Name] Advocate for liberty and personal freedom

Title: The Case for Complete Abolition of State-Recognized and Regulated Marriage

Introduction

The institution of marriage has been a cornerstone of societies throughout history, serving as a fundamental unit for social organization and the foundation for family life. However, its evolving definition and the constant debates surrounding its recognition and regulation have led some to question the need for state involvement in this deeply personal relationship. This essay believes that marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract. By doing so, the state can uphold individual liberties, promote equality, and foster a more inclusive society.

  1. Individual Liberties

The first argument for the complete abolition of state-recognized and regulated marriage is the preservation of individual liberties. Marriage, as a contract between two consenting adults, should not require the state's approval or interference. The current legal framework imposes unnecessary restrictions on individuals' personal choices, infringing upon their right to self-determination and autonomy. By privatizing marriage, the state would respect individuals' freedom to choose how to structure their relationships and uphold their fundamental right to privacy.

The state's involvement in marriage also creates disparities between married and unmarried individuals, as well as between different types of marriages. State recognition of marriage grants certain rights, benefits, and privileges to married partners that are not afforded to unmarried individuals. This differentiation unfairly discriminates against those who choose not to marry or are unable to marry, such as polyamorous individuals. By eliminating state recognition of marriage, these preferential treatments would cease, leveling the playing field and ensuring equal treatment for all individuals.

  1. Promoting Equality

Complete abolition of state-recognized and regulated marriage would also foster greater equality within society. The current system of state-recognized marriage perpetuates inequality by favoring certain types of relationships over others. For instance, the historical exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage has led to disparities in legal rights and societal acceptance between heterosexual and homosexual couples. Even after the legalization of same-sex marriage, the continued use of the term "traditional marriage" to describe heterosexual unions reinforces this hierarchy.

Furthermore, the notion of state-regulated marriage imposes a one-size-fits-all model that does not accommodate the diverse needs and desires of various couples. For example, some marriages may be based on religious beliefs, while others may not. By detaching marriage from the legal sphere and treating it as a private contract, couples would have the freedom to customize their relationships according to their unique situations, beliefs, and preferences. This would eliminate the perpetuation of inequality inherent in the current system and instead promote a more egalitarian society in which all relationships are treated with equal respect and dignity.

  1. Inclusivity and Adaptability

The third argument for abolishing state-regulated marriage is its potential to foster inclusivity and adaptability. The legal boundaries of marriage have long been contested and subject to change, reflecting shifting societal attitudes and values. The state's role in defining and recognizing marriage has often led to exclusionary practices, such as the historical legal prohibition of interracial and same-sex marriages. By removing the state from marriage, the definition of marriage would no longer be subject to political debates or legislative changes, allowing it to evolve organically in response to changing societal norms.

This inclusivity would particularly benefit nontraditional relationships, such as polyamorous partnerships, which the current legal framework does not recognize or legitimize. By privatizing marriage, these relationships would no longer be ostracized or marginalized but would instead be afforded equal legitimacy and rights. This would promote a more accepting and diverse society, uniting individuals rather than dividing them based on arbitrary legal categories.

  1. Legal and Practical Simplification

Lastly, removing the state's involvement in marriage would simplify the legal and practical aspects of personal relationships. The current system necessitates numerous legal proceedings, such as obtaining marriage licenses and negotiating prenuptial agreements, all of which can be time-consuming and costly. A private contract approach would streamline these processes, allowing couples to outline their rights, responsibilities, and expectations in a straightforward manner that suits their individual needs.

Additionally, the dissolution of marriages, or divorces, can be legally complex and emotionally draining, with couples often forced to navigate lengthy court battles and protracted negotiations. In contrast, a private contract approach would allow couples to determine the terms of their separation amicably and efficiently, reducing unnecessary strain and conflict.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the complete abolition of state-recognized and regulated marriage would uphold individual liberties, promote equality, foster inclusivity, and simplify the legal and practical aspects of personal relationships. While the abolition of state-recognized marriage may seem radical, it is a necessary step towards an equal and inclusive society in which relationships are governed by the individuals involved, not the state. By detaching marriage from the legal sphere, the state can focus on its role as a neutral arbiter, ensuring the fair treatment of all citizens without imposing arbitrary boundaries on personal relationships. It is only through this separation that we can truly achieve the goal of "marriage equality" and treat all individuals with the dignity and respect they deserve.

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, asserting that marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract.
Model Response:

Abolish Legal Marriage: The Case for Privatizing the Most Intimate Contract

Introduction
For two centuries the state has claimed a monopolistic right to define, license, and dissolve the relationship we call “marriage.” Politicians, clerks, and judges decide who may marry, on what terms, how wealth moves when it ends, and even which intimate partnerships deserve the word at all. The resulting battles—over inter-racial marriage, no-fault divorce, polygamy, same-sex marriage, polyamory, tax penalties, immigration fraud, and now “weddiquette” for transgender citizens—are not quirks of democracy; they are predictable pathologies of letting governments manage a sphere of life that is quintessentially private. It is time to abolish civil marriage: to remove every statute that creates the legal category of “marriage,” to retire every government form that demands marital status, and to treat adult intimate affiliations exactly as the law now treats friendships, chess clubs, and business partnerships—through voluntary contract and ordinary tort, property, and constitutional law. Marriage should be returned to the realm of culture, conscience, and community where it was born. The state’s only legitimate role is to enforce the contracts people freely choose and to protect the vulnerable from force and fraud.

I. The Myth of Neutrality: How the State Invented the Culture War
When the government labels some relationships “marriage,” it unavoidably takes sides in moral and theological disputes. The moment a legislature writes a definition, it creates insiders and outsiders. In 1958 Mildred and Richard Loving could not marry in Virginia because the Racial Integrity Act criminalized inter-racial unions; their relationship was deemed “unnatural.” In 2015 Kentucky clerk Kim Davis refused to license same-sex marriages because her Bible called them “unnatural.” Same actor (the state), same mechanism (the marriage license), different victims. The only constant is coercion.

Legal marriage is therefore not a neutral institution that merely “records” people’s commitments; it is a value-laden gatekeeper that distributes honor, legitimacy, and material perks. There is no neutral definition available. Expand the definition to include same-sex couples, and you still exclude three-person units, sibling households, long-term cohabitants who reject the word “marriage,” or platonic partners who share finances and child-rearing. Continue expanding and the category dissolves into meaninglessness; contract law is the only residue that remains. Abolition skips the endless, zero-sum game of deciding whose love is “real” and moves directly to that residue.

II. The Injustice of the Marriage Bonus
Each year the federal government dispenses over 500 statutory benefits—tax breaks, Social Security survivor payments, immigration preferences, veterans’ spousal allowances, hospital visitation default rules, family-leave guarantees—on the basis of a single credential: a state marriage license. These benefits are not free; they are financed by the unmarried, who subsidize strangers’ weddings through higher taxes and foregone opportunities. The Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center calculates that in 2022 a middle-income, one-earner couple received an average bonus of $1,660 compared with two unmarried peers, while dual-earner cohabitants often face a penalty. A solo mother earning $30,000 and caring for an elderly parent receives neither the tax bonus nor the Social Security bump granted to a married stockbroker. The system is overtly redistributive—away from gays in 1980, away from singles today, away from immigrants tomorrow. No liberal society should redistribute wealth on the basis of amorous labels.

III. Family Law as Moral Police
Family courts claim jurisdiction over whom you may sleep with (adultery remains a factor in alimony in half the states), how you raise your children (religious upbringing clauses in custody orders), and even your post-divorce dating life (“morality clauses” routinely forbid overnight guests of the opposite sex). These rulings are possible only because the state has inserted itself into the marital bedroom. Once marriage is privatized, courts would lose the doctrinal hook for such intrusions. Child custody would hinge on the best-interest standard applied to each parent, not on the existential question, “Was this marriage valid?” Spousal support would be enforceable only if the parties voluntarily contracted for it, just as business partners may, but need not, agree to post-dissipation payments. Religious communities would regain authority to impose spiritual sanctions (or not) without embroiling the rest of us in their disciplines.

IV. The False Necessity Argument: “But How Will We track Property, Inheritance, or Medical Decisions?”
Critics contend that without civil marriage, society would collapse into litigation anarchy. The claim is historically and comparatively false. Anglo-American law handled property, inheritance, and guardianship for centuries before the marriage-license regime was invented in the mid-1800s. Today five jurisdictions—New Zealand, Australia, Sweden, Colorado, and California—already allow any two adults to register as “domestic partners” or “civil union” without romantic prerequisites, proving that the administrative work of marriage (survivorship, default inheritance, next-of-kin status) can be disentangled from the sentimental branding.

Privatization simply extends the logic already familiar in other arenas:

  1. Default Inheritance: If you die intestate, your estate passes under a statutory schedule—currently to “spouse first, then issue.” Replace “spouse” with “registered primary beneficiary,” allow online registration, and the identical social objective is met without policing bedrooms.
  2. Medical Decisions: Hospitals already honor Medical Powers of Attorney. A one-page statutory form, available in every language, could create the same presumptive authority that marriage currently provides.
  3. Property Sharing: Unmarried co-owners already buy houses, co-sign mortgages, and partition real estate through contract and partition statutes. Abolishing civil marriage merely universalizes the contractual regime now available only to the litigation-savvy.
  4. Child Support and Custody: Courts decide parentage and best-interest matters for never-married parents every day; nothing about that analysis depends on the existence of a marriage license.
  5. Immigration: Replace the “marriage visa” with a “co-sponsorship visa.” Any citizen may co-sponsor one additional adult, assuming financial liability, subject to fraud penalties. The market for green-card paparazzi marriages disappears overnight.

V. Liberty, Equality, Privacy: Abolition as Constitutional Imperative
The First Amendment forbids government establishment of religion; yet marriage licensing enforces canonical definitions contested by Protestant, Catholic, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, and secular citizens alike. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees equal protection; yet marriage laws overtly discriminate on the basis of marital status, sexual orientation, number of partners, and even age (with parental-consent exceptions that do not apply to other contracts). The Supreme Court’s 2003 Lawrence v. Texas decision recognized that adults have a liberty interest in choosing intimate associations. The most straightforward way to vindicate that principle is to stop issuing licenses for intimacy altogether. Abolition transforms every citizen from supplicant to rights-bearer: the state no longer “allows” you to marry; it simply enforces whateverprivate agreements you craft.

VI. Feminist and Queer Liberation Through Contract
Early feminists such as Emma Goldman and Voltairine de Cleyre opposed state marriage as “the ownership of the woman by the man.” Contemporary feminists critique the “marriage premium” that pushes women into economically dependent relationships. Privatization allows tailor-made contracts: a couple may choose community property or strict separation, may agree to compensate unpaid care work, may stipulate mutually negotiated exit terms, or may refuse any contract at all and keep finances separate. Likewise, queer theorists warn that assimilation into the marriage paradigm erases radical pluralism. Abolition keeps the promise of Obergefell—equal dignity—while avoiding the assimilationist vise. LGBTQ citizens, polyamorous networks, or celibate best friends may register whatever consortium they wish, on their own moral terms.

VII. Economic Efficiency: Abolition as Deregulation
Marriage is the most heavily regulated industry most Americans ever enter, yet it is never audited for cost-benefit balance. County clerks, divorce courts, marital-master programs, and federal joint-return compliance consume billions in tax expenditures. The wedding-license bureaucracy alone costs an estimated $600 million annually. Private contract, standardized forms, and online registration would shrink these expenses to a rounding error. Businesses would also gain clarity: employers currently juggle conflicting state definitions when determining spousal health benefits, pension payouts, and relocation assistance. A uniform contractual default—enforceable in any court—would cut HR compliance costs and end the cross-border moral arbitrage in which companies relocate to states with narrower marriage rules.

VIII. Objections Answered

  1. “Marriage protects women who sacrifice careers.”
    Postnuptial agreements, default partnership rules, and social insurance can compensate care-givers without licensing love. Sweden’s gender-neutral caregiver allowance and Quebec’s universal child-benefit show that public policy can reward labor, not labels.

  2. “The poor can’t afford lawyers to draft contracts.”
    The solution is publicly funded templates (as we provide for wills, divorce petitions, and small-claims forms), not the retention of a coercive licensing regime for everyone. A one-page “Standard Intimate Partnership” form could be downloaded at libraries and filed for free.

  3. “Marriage tames men and civilizes society.”
    The claim is empirically weak: crime rates, domestic violence, and out-of-wedlock births vary far more with employment, education, and inequality than with marriage rates. Norway’s non-marital birthrate is 56 percent, yet its homicide rate is one-eighth that of the United States. Social stability is produced by prosperity and rule of law, not by state sanctification of dyads.

  4. “Religious groups will lose the sacrament.”
    On the contrary, privatization liberates religion. Catholics may refuse remarriage after divorce; Reform rabbis may bless same-sex unions; Mormon off-shoots may practice polygamy (subject to ordinary contract law). The state neither endorses nor penalizes any of these choices, restoring authentic pluralism.

IX. Transition: How We Get There

  1. Phase 1: Automatic Conversion. Every existing marriage license is deemed a “Standard Intimate Partnership Contract” with the identical rights and obligations, but parties may opt out by mutual written notice within two years.
  2. Phase 2: Statutory Rewrite. All federal and state codes replace “spouse” with “registered designated partner,” defined as “any adult who has filed an Affidavit of Mutual Responsibility.” The affidavit requires notarization, not solemnization.
  3. Phase 3: Sunset the License. County clerks cease issuing marriage licenses; wedding ceremonies become purely ceremonial. Religious officiants perform sacraments without filing state documents; couples who want legal consequences execute a contract.
  4. Phase 4: Equalize the Tax Code. All references to filing status are repealed; every individual files on personal income, with deductions for actual dependents. Social Security converts to individual accounts with survivorship payable to any designated beneficiary.
  5. Phase 5: Educational Campaign. High-school curricula teach contract literacy, so every citizen learns how to create, modify, or dissolve partnership agreements.

X. Conclusion: From Permission Right to Liberty Right
Two visions confront us. In the first, the state continues to license intimacy, ensuring that every new generation fights the same culture war under a different flag—today gay marriage, tomorrow robot marriage, the day after incestuous genetics. In the second vision, the state bows out, enforcing contracts and protecting the weak while leaving sacred and erotic meanings to conscience and community. The second vision is not utopian; it is merely the extension of the liberal principle that consenting adults should arrange their own lives unless they harm third parties.

Abolishing civil marriage does not devalue commitment; it elevates it. When two people sign a partnership affidavit before friends and family, they are not asking a bureaucrat for permission; they are promising each other, in Goldman’s words, “life and love until death,” backed by their own moral codes and by the neutral enforcement of voluntary promises. The state’s proper role is to keep the peace, not to preside over weddings. Let judges deal with fraud, duress, and abuse; let poets, priests, and punk-rock officiants decide what love requires. It is time to end the era of marriage licenses and begin the era of free contracts.

Abolition returns the default to “strangers” and lets the two adults pick every clause à-la-carte (cohabitation contract, medical-power-of-attorney, will, partnership deed, sexual-exclusivity covenant—or none at all).
  • Plural life-styles cease to be “exceptions.” Whether the household is monogamous, polyamorous, celibate, childless, or a “throuple” is irrelevant to public law; no configuration is privileged or penalized.
  • Exit equality. Because there is no special “family court,” dissolution is handled like any other contract dispute or, if no contract exists, like the break-up of roommates. Neither party can invoke the state to obtain lifetime alimony or a presumptive 50 % share of the other’s earnings.
  1. Government overreach
  • Ends the hidden subsidy stream. Joint tax filing, spousal Social Security, veteran’s benefits, and employer mandates are transparent transfers from the unmarried to the married. Removing the category eliminates the transfer; the state no longer nudges people toward one household form.
  • Shrinks administrative bureaucracy. County clerks, marriage-license systems, federal “married” check-boxes on 100+ forms, and the IRS’s 200-page “Publication 17” marriage-income examples all disappear. Pension systems no longer need “survivor” rules that require actuarial cross-subsidies.
  • Gets the state out of moral grading. Legislatures would no longer decide which relationships are “worthy” (e.g., cousin vs. same-sex vs. polygamous). Culture wars over the definition of marriage become purely cultural—no winners or losers in tax or immigration codes.
  1. Purely private ordering
  • Competitive contract templates. Religious bodies, secular non-profits, and commercial insurers could offer pre-drafted “marriage 2.0” bundles (Orthodox ketubah-plus, Catholic indissoluble covenant, polyamorous rotating-partner deed, etc.). Reputational intermediaries—analogous to ISO safety standards—would certify which contracts are clear, fair, and arbitrated by reputable private tribunals.
  • Opt-in dependant designations. Every “spousal” privilege now written in statute (hospital visitation, health-insurance eligibility, intestate inheritance, immigration sponsorship) becomes an explicit form anyone can file—directed to the actual person they want covered, whether lover, cousin, best friend, or platonic co-parent. Insurers and hospitals have incentives to accept such designations because the customer, not the Treasury, pays.
  • Children’s status is already independent. Paternity law, child-support guidelines, and guardianship proceedings exist separately from marriage; abolition leaves them untouched. What disappears is the automatic presumption that a spouse is also a second parent; that link is created by explicit adoption or parentage orders, which many reformers see as more accurate anyway.

Common objections and the libertarian reply

  • “Chaos—everyone will write incompatible contracts.” Standardized forms already dominate the private economy (credit-card agreements, property deeds, software licenses). Markets converge on a handful of dominant templates; the same would occur for pair-bond contracts.
  • “Gold-diggers left penniless.” Anyone who wants economic protection can bargain for it up-front or refuse to cohabit. The abolitionist sees that as empowerment, not cruelty.
  • “Immigration fraud.” Replace marriage-based visas with a market-priced sponsorship bond: a citizen posts a substantial bail that is forfeit if the sponsored immigrant becomes a public charge. Love is irrelevant; solvency is demonstrable.
  • “Religious groups will lose ‘marriage’.” On the contrary: churches, mosques, and temples would own the word outright. The state’s retreat privatizes the symbolism; no one can sue a church to force it to solemnize any particular union, because the unions are now legally meaningless.

Bottom line
Legal abolition of marriage does not prohibit weddings, rings, vows, or life-long commitment. It merely removes the state’s power to confer special status and special obligations on some households but not others. It treats adults as fully competent to craft their own intimate law, turns every “spousal” privilege into a freely chosen designation, and depoliticizes an institution that has become a lightning rod for culture-war rent-seeking. In the slogan favored by libertarian scholars: “Keep the promise; lose the license.”
