Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, asserting that marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract.
Model Response:

What if the state simply stopped licensing love? For centuries governments have granted, withheld, and configured special legal status for a social practice that long predates them: marriage. That choice has shaped taxes, property, immigration, healthcare, inheritance, custody, even criminal procedure. It has also produced endless moral conflict, discrimination, loopholes, and coercive incentives. The simplest and most principled solution is to remove marriage from the legal sphere entirely and treat intimate partnerships solely as private relationships or contracts. The state should enforce general duties (to children, to creditors, to victims of abuse) and general agreements people make—nothing more and nothing less. Doing so would honor freedom, reduce conflict, and produce clearer, fairer law.

The principled case: neutrality, autonomy, and equality

  • Liberal neutrality. A liberal state should not pick winners among conceptions of the good life. By recognizing “marriage” as a privileged civil status, the state elevates one model of intimacy—romantic, dyadic, long-term cohabitation—over others: non-romantic caregiving partnerships, plural households, lifelong friendships, multi-generational arrangements, and solitary lives. Government neutrality requires withdrawing from this moral endorsement business and letting people organize their private associations as they wish.
  • Personal autonomy. Adults should structure their commitments according to their values, not the state’s template. A wedding can remain a religious sacrament or a secular rite, but the legal implications should arise only from explicit agreements, not from a license that drags a thousand default consequences behind it. Freedom of contract respects diversity better than one-size-fits-all family law.
  • Equal citizenship. Tying benefits and recognition to marital status privileges some citizens over others. Singles, widows, aromantic people, roommates who share burdens, and adult children caring for parents are disadvantaged in taxes, benefits, hospital visitation, and housing rules. Abolishing civil marriage would end marital privilege and refocus policy on needs, caregiving, and dependency rather than on whether two people said “I do.”

The historical case: a bad track record of state-defined marriage

  • State power over marriage has repeatedly been an instrument of oppression and social control: bans on interracial marriage, prohibitions on same-sex marriage, coverture doctrines that erased married women’s legal personhood, and marital-rape exemptions that protected abusers. Even where reforms have corrected injustices, the core problem persists: when the state defines marriage, it invites political majorities to impose their moral views on intimate life.
  • Each “victory” in the marriage culture wars spawns the next battlefield—who counts as a spouse, what benefits attach, how many spouses are permitted, which religious or cultural forms qualify. The recurring conflict is not a bug but a feature of state recognition itself. The surest way to end the wars is to disarm the battlefield.

The practical case: clarity, fairness, and fewer perverse incentives

  • Cleaner law. Today’s marriage status collapses dozens of unrelated legal issues—tax filing, hospital visitation, inheritance, immigration, evidentiary privilege—into a single checkbox. This creates distortions. Couples may marry to gain a tax bonus, a visa, or health insurance, not because their relationship fits the traditional template. Detangle the law: handle each legal interest with the right instrument.
  • Fair taxation and benefits. Replace marital filing statuses and spousal bonuses/penalties with individual-based taxation and household-based credits tied to dependents and caregiving. Benefits should reward what society aims to support—raising children, supporting disabled relatives, sharing housing costs—rather than a romantic label.
  • Reduced administrative burdens and litigation. Family courts devote massive resources to sorting property, support, and custody through the special machinery of divorce. Under a contract-based system, property sharing and support obligations are governed by the agreements people actually make, with default contract templates for those who want them. Child-related matters are adjudicated under a unified parenthood regime, the same regardless of the parents’ relationship history.
  • Inclusion without exception. When policy hinges on marriage, governments must constantly decide who qualifies, producing edge-case unfairness: fiancés, long-term roommates, polycules, sibling caregivers, and other household forms fall through the cracks. A status-neutral approach lets each person designate beneficiaries, proxies, and cohabitants without pretending every arrangement is “marriage.”

“But what about the children?” A better, marriage-free framework Protecting children is a legitimate state interest. We do not need marital status to do it.

  • Parenthood, not partnership. The law should attach rights and duties to parenthood—established by birth, acknowledgment, adjudication, or adoption—rather than to the parents’ relationship with each other. Child support, custody, and parental decision-making are then governed by a single, coherent regime.
  • Clear defaults. Statutes can define default rules for parental responsibility and support, applicable to any parent regardless of their romantic history. Courts already handle these questions for unmarried parents; eliminating marital status simply removes arbitrary discrepancies.
  • Support for caregiving. Public benefits aimed at children—tax credits, childcare subsidies, health coverage—should depend on the presence of dependents and income, not on whether caregivers are married.

“How would people get the practical rights spouses now enjoy?” With precise tools instead of a blunt instrument.

  • Property and inheritance. Anyone can designate beneficiaries by will, create joint tenancy for shared property, and use beneficiary forms for insurance and retirement accounts. Where people want shared-earnings regimes, they can adopt a standard cohabitation or partnership agreement.
  • Health care and hospital access. Replace “spouse-first” defaults with a simple, universal hierarchy that begins with the patient’s designated health-care proxy and visitation list. Everyone, married or not, should name these designees—no wedding ring required.
  • Decision-making and privacy. Allow each adult to designate one or more “confidants” with decision and access rights, replacing spousal privileges with a wider, non-discriminatory system. Evidentiary privileges can be extended to designated intimates rather than only to spouses.
  • Immigration. Tie family-reunification to demonstrable dependency, caregiving, and household integration rather than marital status. Allow sponsorship of partners, parents, or other household members subject to financial guarantees and fraud screening, not a marriage certificate.
  • Violence and exploitation. Domestic violence law already extends beyond spouses to dating partners and cohabitants. Keep and strengthen that status-neutral protection. Abuse is about power and harm, not marital titles.

Contracts instead of licenses: a simple, protective architecture To make privatized relationships workable and fair, lawmakers can provide:

  • Standardized private agreements. Government publishes model cohabitation, caregiving, and property-sharing templates that people can adopt, customize, or ignore. They set expectations up front, reduce disputes, and are enforced by ordinary contract law. No special “family” status is conferred.
  • Designation registries. Not a marriage registry, but simple, low-cost registries (or secure digital tools) for health-care proxies, beneficiaries for state-managed benefits, next-of-kin contacts, and household co-signers. These are like existing organ-donor or emergency-contact systems—neutral, non-moral, and universally available.
  • Robust defaults for the uncontracted. Where people fail to plan, general default rules can mitigate hardship—for example, presumptions about co-owned household goods or reimbursement for contributions to shared property. These are narrow and purpose-built, not blanket marital regimes.

Answering common objections

  • “Marriage promotes stability.” Stability flows from commitment, compatibility, and economic security, not from a government certificate. Where policy can foster stability—through childcare, housing affordability, and caregiver support—it should do so directly. The marriage proxy is crude and exclusionary.
  • “Abolition will increase litigation.” Much litigation arises because marital status bundles property, support, and custody into high-stakes, all-or-nothing disputes. Clarifying contracts and separating child issues from adult romance can reduce conflict by aligning legal processes with the actual interests at stake.
  • “Religious communities need civil marriage.” They can retain sacramental marriage, with full freedom to define it according to their doctrines. Abolition of civil marriage eliminates coercion in both directions: religious bodies do not have to alter their rites to track civil requirements, and non-adherents are not bound by religiously inflected civil norms.
  • “This is too radical.” We already live much of this reality. Unmarried partners raise children, own property, and plan estates. Courts adjudicate parenthood without regard to marital status. Employers let workers designate beneficiaries and emergency contacts. Abolition simply makes the law coherent and principled.

A feasible transition

  • Grandfather existing marriages. Recognize current marriages as private civil contracts with the same terms unless the parties opt to convert to a new agreement, ensuring no one loses relied-upon protections.
  • Sunset licensing. Stop issuing new marriage licenses after a transition date while expanding access to designation tools and standard contracts.

Here are the main reasons and supposed benefits often cited for abolishing all legal recognition of marriage and treating it purely as a private matter.

Respect for individual autonomy

  • Freedom to define relationships: Adults can design their own arrangements (property-sharing, support, caregiving, exclusivity, household rules) via contract rather than accept a one-size-fits-all marital status.
  • Consent and exit: Parties choose obligations they actually want and can opt out without navigating a state-defined dissolution regime; reduces paternalistic defaults that bind people who never consented to them.
  • Privacy and dignity: Intimate life is not registered, licensed, or disclosed to the state; fewer public records and fewer third-party demands to see “marital status.”
  • Pluralism: Accommodates diverse forms—cohabitation, poly households, chosen families, religious unions—without the state endorsing or condemning any particular model.
  • Reduced coercion: People aren’t pressured to marry to access benefits (health insurance, taxes, immigration), making relationship choices more authentic.

Reduced government overreach

  • No licensing of intimacy: The state stops approving, denying, or policing adult romantic/household arrangements.
  • Smaller bureaucracy and surveillance: Eliminates registrars, verification checks, and investigations into “real” versus “sham” marriages across taxes, immigration, and benefits.
  • Fewer culture-war flashpoints: The state no longer defines “marriage,” defusing conflicts over who qualifies; clearer separation of church and state.
  • Less litigation over status: Avoids interstate recognition fights, religious exemptions battles, and disputes over who counts as a spouse; focuses courts on concrete claims (contract, property, unjust enrichment).
  • Neutrality in public policy: Laws can protect children and dependents directly rather than indirectly via a marital category.

Treating marriage as a private matter

  • Contract-based arrangements: Couples or households use standard contracts (or customized ones) for property sharing, support, dispute resolution, and exit terms; consumer-protection rules can ensure informed consent and fairness.
  • Designated-beneficiary systems: Simple forms determine hospital visitation, medical decision-making, inheritance, death benefits, and next-of-kin—without needing a marital status.
  • Individual-based public benefits and taxes: Eligibility and rates are set per person (or per dependent), removing marriage bonuses/penalties and the need to verify spousal status.
  • Parentage law focused on children: Clear, status-neutral rules for establishing parentage, custody, support, and caregiving responsibilities regardless of the adults’ relationship.
  • Workplace and insurance neutrality: Employers offer benefits to an employee’s designated dependent(s) or provide cash equivalents; insurers allow household or named-dependent coverage without requiring “spouse” proof.
  • Religious and cultural freedom: Faith communities can perform and recognize marriages as they wish, without state endorsement or constraint; others can opt for secular ceremonies or none at all.

Equality and fairness

  • Ends marital privilege: Singles, cohabitants, multi-adult households, and asexual or aromantic individuals aren’t disadvantaged relative to married pairs.
  • Eliminates incentives and penalties: Tax and welfare systems stop nudging people toward or away from marriage; fewer accusations of “marriage fraud.”
  • Inclusive by design: Avoids recurring fights over expanding the marital category (e.g., same-sex, polyamorous) because the law doesn’t rely on the category in the first place.

Administrative and economic benefits

  • Simpler rules and fewer disputes: Agencies stop adjudicating marital status; eligibility checks become document-based (designations, contracts).
  • Lower compliance costs: HR departments and government offices process fewer spousal-specific forms; benefits become portable and person-centered.
  • Clearer risk allocation: Private contracts specify expectations, reducing uncertainty about support and property division.

Refocusing law on genuine vulnerabilities

  • Direct protection for dependents: The law targets what matters—children’s welfare, caregiving obligations to disabled dependents, prevention of exploitation—without using marriage as a proxy.
  • Tailored defaults: Where parties do nothing, neutral, opt-out default rules (for cohabitation property, caregiving, and estates) can provide baseline fairness without imposing a marital template.

In short, abolishing legal marriage aims to maximize adult autonomy, minimize government control over intimate life, and depoliticize family structure by replacing a status-based system with voluntary contracts, designated-beneficiary choices, and child-focused parentage rules. Proponents see this as fairer, more private, and more administratively coherent than tying wide swaths of law and benefits to a state-defined marital status.

Question:
Draft a passionate speech that strongly advocates for completely abolishing state recognition and regulation of marriage in order to protect personal freedom and remove government interference from private relationships.
Model Response:

Friends, neighbors, and fellow citizens,

We have been told that the state belongs in our courthouses, our schools, our roads—places where our shared life requires common rules. But for too long, the state has also claimed space in our most intimate territory: our private relationships. It has turned love into a license, commitment into a category, and family into a box checked or left blank. Tonight I stand before you to say, with conviction and hope, that it is time to abolish state recognition and regulation of marriage. Not to weaken families, but to strengthen freedom. Not to erode responsibility, but to ground it in consent and conscience. Not to attack tradition, but to liberate it from the cold machinery of government.

Marriage long predates the modern state. It has been a covenant, a sacrament, a celebration, a rite of passage—a tapestry woven by cultures, faiths, and families across centuries. The state did not invent it. Yet over time, the state claimed it, codified it, licensed it, and—let us be honest—weaponized it. It used marriage to control women’s property and bodies. It used marriage to police interracial love. It used marriage to exclude same-sex couples from dignity and protection. It used marriage to ration social benefits and to reward some households while punishing others. It has always been a gatekeeper, and gatekeepers always close more doors than they open.

A free people should not need a permission slip to love, to build a household, to share property, or to promise fidelity. A free people should not fear that a change in political winds can suddenly redraw the boundaries of who counts as a family. If the most intimate decision two—or more—consenting adults can make requires state approval, then our freedom is conditional. And conditional freedom is not freedom at all.

Consider the absurdity: the state cannot certify sincerity, yet it issues sincerity’s license. It cannot guarantee fidelity, yet it stamps fidelity’s seal. It cannot bestow dignity, yet it doles out dignity’s benefits. Government is good at mediating harms and enforcing contracts. It is not good at sanctifying love.

Some will say: “But the law must protect people.” I agree. That is precisely why marriage should no longer be a legal status. When protections depend on a marital status the state defines, those outside the line are left exposed. Protection should attach to people and to promises, not to a box labeled “spouse.” We can build a better, fairer civil framework—one that covers everyone, with or without a ceremony.

Here is what that looks like:

First, we shift from licensing status to enforcing consent. Adults can enter private relationship and household contracts—standardized, accessible, and enforceable—covering property, support, decision-making, and custody. No theology, no ideology, just clear terms. Courts already enforce contracts every day. Let them do it here.

Second, we decouple public benefits from marital status. Employer health plans, tax preferences, housing rights, immigration sponsorship, hospital visitation, medical decision-making—these should flow from designated dependents and household relationships, not a marriage certificate. Each adult can name the loved ones who rely on them. Benefits become portable, inclusive, and fair.

Third, we modernize default protections. Not everyone will write a contract. That’s reality. So the law can supply default rules for cohabiting partners and shared households—clear, opt-out defaults that define property sharing, responsibilities, and next-of-kin status. Domestic violence laws must and can continue to protect anyone in intimate or household relationships. Child support and parental obligations flow from parentage and caregiving, not from whether adults said “I do.”

Fourth, we respect religious freedom and cultural tradition. Faith communities may solemnize marriage as sacrament. Families may celebrate marriage as custom. Nothing in this vision prohibits private vows, communal rituals, or lifelong covenants. It simply ends the state’s role as celebrant-in-chief. Your love does not need a government seal; your faith does not need a state stamp.

Fifth, we provide a humane transition. Existing civil marriages can be grandfathered or converted into private contracts with the same rights and obligations. Statutes that say “spouse” can be revised to say “designated partner,” “dependent,” or “household member” as appropriate. No one loses protection; everyone gains freedom.

To the skeptics who worry this will “weaken the family,” I ask: what makes a family strong? Is it a license, or is it love and responsibility? Families are built by care, not by categories; by daily acts of devotion, not by clerks at a counter. If a relationship cannot stand without a state’s blessing, it was never strong. If a relationship is strong, it should not need the state’s blessing to endure.

To those who fear the vulnerable will be left behind, consider who is left behind now: the partner of decades shut out of a hospital room; the caretaker friend excluded from bereavement leave; the single parent navigating a system stacked against “non-traditional” households; the survivor whose abuser is shielded by marital privilege; the legal stranger denied inheritance because love did not fit the law’s mold. Abolishing state marriage does not abandon protection—it ends the rationing of protection. It turns a narrow doorway into a wide gate.

To those who say the state must celebrate love to honor society’s values, I answer: that is not the state’s job. The state must protect liberty, adjudicate disputes, and prevent harm. Celebration belongs to communities. Sanctification belongs to faiths. Recognition belongs to one another. You do not need a senator’s signature to make a promise that matters. You do not need a judge’s robe to know your family is real.

Imagine a society where your household’s legal security does not hinge on your conformity to a historic norm. Imagine a tax code that treats you as an individual, not as a category to be engineered. Imagine employers who recognize the dependents you actually support. Imagine hospitals that use your explicit consent documents, not guesswork based on titles. Imagine courts that enforce your promises because you made them, not because the state approved your relationship.

This is not a utopia; it is a set of practical reforms well within our reach. We already allow medical proxies. We already honor wills. We already enforce contracts. We already recognize domestic violence beyond marital bonds. We already acknowledge that love and care take many forms. The change is simply this: we stop pretending the state can declare which of those forms is legitimate.

When the state can declare who counts as married, it can also declare who does not. And whenever government is given an on-switch over our private lives, it eventually finds the off-switch. Freedom demands that we remove both.

So let us be bold. Let us retire the license and keep the love. Let us replace marital status with clear contracts, fair defaults, and universal protections. Let us stop measuring families by paperwork and start honoring them by the responsibilities they shoulder. Let us finally separate love and state.

I ask you to join me—citizens, lawmakers, judges, employers, faith leaders—in a simple, powerful commitment: no more government gatekeeping over our private relationships. Repeal civil marriage as a legal status. Decouple benefits from marital categories. Build a civil framework that protects people because they are people, not because they fit a form.

No more licenses for love. No more gatekeepers for dignity. No more state permission slips for the most human promise we can make.

Our lives are ours. Our promises are ours. Our families are ours. Let’s keep it that way.

Abolishing State-Regulated Marriage: The Case for Complete Legal Separation

For centuries, marriage has existed both as a deeply personal relationship and as a legally regulated institution. Governments across the world have tied a wide range of legal rights, benefits, and obligations to one’s marital status, intertwining personal relationships with political bureaucracy. While historically justified as a means of organizing property, inheritance, and social stability, the modern system of state-recognized marriage is an unnecessary vestige of an era when governments sought to control intimate affairs. In a pluralistic, individual-rights–oriented society, there is no valid justification for the state to dictate or define who is “married.” Marriage is fundamentally a private human contract, rooted in personal commitment and mutual consent — and it should be removed from the legal sphere entirely.

This isn’t simply a call for “marriage equality” under state law; it is an assertion that the state should have no role at all in marriage, regardless of the genders, identities, or arrangements involved. The abolition of state-recognized marriage would not diminish freedom — it would expand it for everyone.

I. Marriage Is a Personal, Not Political, Relationship

At its core, marriage is a voluntary bond between individuals. For some, it is a religious sacrament; for others, a purely emotional commitment; still for others, a social or cultural tradition. None of these dimensions require political oversight. Government involvement in marriage assumes that the state has the moral authority to validate, regulate, and even dissolve intimate relationships. But such authority is unjustifiable — after all, the state does not issue licenses for friendship, nor does it regulate the emotional bonds of parent-child relationships beyond essential protections against harm.

By privatizing marriage — treating it as a personal agreement between consenting adults — the bond would be a matter of free association, just like any other private contractual or religious arrangement. Individuals could negotiate the terms of their commitment, structure their household as they see fit, and seek mediation or arbitration in the event of disputes without ever needing to secure government “approval.”

II. State-Defined Marriage Creates Inequality by Design

Contrary to the belief that legal marriage promotes fairness, the structure of state-defined marriage artificially privileges a certain type of relationship at the expense of others. Married couples often receive special tax benefits, inheritance rights, immigration opportunities, and healthcare decision-making powers unavailable to unmarried individuals, no matter the longevity or seriousness of their relationships. This creates a two-tiered system where the government rewards one specific model of family or partnership while ignoring — or actively disadvantaging — alternatives.

Private contractual agreements could provide all necessary legal mechanisms for rights such as hospital visitation, inheritance, and shared property ownership, without the state reserving such privileges for only those who meet its definition of “married.” Abolishing state-recognized marriage would thus eliminate legal favoritism and allow all relationships to be treated equitably, regardless of form.

III. Removing Marriage From Law Would Reduce Cultural Conflict

Much of the public divisiveness over marriage law — especially in recent decades — has stemmed from the fact that the state acts as the arbiter of which relationships are legitimate. Conflicts over whether same-sex couples, plural unions, or non-traditional arrangements should be legally recognized arise precisely because legal recognition is exclusive. If the state were completely uninvolved, political disputes over “who can marry” would vanish, because there would be no state license to fight over.

By privatizing marriage, debates about legitimacy would shift from political arenas to cultural, religious, or personal contexts, where individuals could freely associate with communities sharing their values without imposing their definitions on others via state power.

IV. Historical Justifications Are No Longer Relevant

Historically, marriage law served practical governance purposes: consolidating property, ensuring paternal certainty in an era before DNA testing, regulating succession and inheritance, and securing alliances. But modern legal and technological systems make these purposes obsolete.

Property law, inheritance law, and parental rights statutes already function without requiring marriage as a prerequisite — and when they still do, it is due to outdated legal frameworks that could easily be reformed. Child custody determinations are handled through family law regardless of marital status; wills and trusts handle inheritance without a marriage license; and advanced reproductive testing removes the need for the presumption of paternity embedded in marriage law. In short: the legal functions marriage once served can already be — and in many cases are — handled by other legal mechanisms without defining, licensing, or privileging the relationship itself.

V. Contract Law Can Replace Marriage Law Entirely

One common concern is that eliminating legal marriage would create uncertainty in cases of divorce, property division, and shared financial obligations. Yet contract law already provides all the tools necessary for handling such matters. Couples, friends, or families could draft relationship contracts specifying financial arrangements, support obligations, or guardianship agreements. These could be as detailed or as simple as the parties desire, tailored to their unique circumstances rather than bound by a one-size-fits-all state marriage code.

If conflicts arise, mediation and the courts could enforce such agreements precisely as they would with any other contract — without state-by-default imposition of marriage-specific obligations that may not reflect the intentions of the individuals involved.

VI. The Moral and Philosophical Argument for Non-Interference

At its heart, this is about autonomy. A free society respects the right of individuals to define their own relationships, provided they do not infringe upon the rights of others. Government involvement in marriage assumes a paternalistic role: implying citizens need official validation for their personal commitments. This runs directly counter to the principles of individual liberty, bodily autonomy, and free association.

The state’s interest should be limited to protecting individuals from harm and enforcing agreements voluntarily entered into — not prescribing the form or content of personal relationships.

Conclusion: Freedom Through Separation

The complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage would liberate human relationships from political control, dismantle legal favoritism, remove perennial cultural conflicts, and reinforce individual liberty. In a society built on the principles of equality and freedom, there is no place for government-sanctioned intimacy.

By treating marriage entirely as a private matter — whether religious, secular, polyamorous, monogamous, or otherwise — we can create a society in which individuals are free to form partnerships that reflect their own values, negotiate their own terms, and live without state intrusion in the most personal areas of their lives. It’s time to remove marriage from the law books and return it to where it belongs: to the people themselves.

"Marriage Belongs to the People, Not the State"

My friends,

People will still make their promises of fidelity and care. Contracts will still make property, inheritance, and guardianship agreements enforceable. The difference is that the State’s permission slip will finally be gone, and with it, an unjust and unnecessary intrusion into private life.

Marriage should be a matter of conscience, not compliance. Of personal choice, not political decree. If we truly believe in the freedom to love, then we must demand the government step aside—and keep its hands off our hearts.

Let us end the era of licensed love. Let us reclaim one of humanity’s oldest institutions for the people to whom it has always truly belonged.

Question:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, asserting that marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract.
Model Response:

Marriage—once a matter of ritual, religious doctrine, or local custom—has long been entangled with the power of the state. Today, governments license weddings, determine who may marry whom, and distribute a vast array of legal rights and benefits tied to the marital label. That arrangement is neither inevitable nor desirable. The state should withdraw entirely from recognizing and regulating marriage: the institution should be removed from the legal sphere and treated instead as a private relationship or contract. This transformation would better protect individual liberty, promote equality, respect pluralism, reduce perverse incentives and bureaucratic costs, and create a clearer, fairer legal framework grounded in consent and contract law.

Individual autonomy and freedom At the core of the case for abolition is a basic liberal ideal: adults should be free to form, define, and dissolve intimate relationships without state imposition. When the state confers special legal meaning on a particular social form—“marriage”—it privileges one model of intimate life and shapes behavior by attaching rewards and penalties. People are nudged, often economically compelled, into a narrow institutional structure in order to obtain healthcare access, inheritance rights, immigration sponsorship, tax advantages, or parental presumptions. Removing the state from the marriage business restores autonomy: individuals and couples could define their relationships and arrange their affairs through private agreements tailored to their needs, values, and cultures, free from a one-size-fits-all legal template.

Equality and dismantling embedded hierarchies State-recognized marriage has historically reinforced exclusionary and patriarchal patterns—defining who counts as a legitimate family, legitimizing gender-based economic dependency, and criminalizing or marginalizing other relationship structures. While many legal reforms have expanded access—most notably the extension of recognition to same-sex couples—state marriage remains a structural privilege that benefits some people more than others and perpetuates inequalities for those who fall outside its bounds (cohabitants, polyamorous groups, non-romantic caregivers, etc.). Abolishing state-sanctioned marriage levels the playing field. Rights and protections would be distributed according to clear, neutral legal principles—contract, property, and parental law—rather than by whether a couple fit a historical or religious template.

Separation of church and state and pluralism For many, marriage is first and foremost a religious or cultural sacrament. The entanglement of religious rites with civil sanction undermines both religious freedom and secular governance. When the state licenses marriages, it implicitly endorses particular conceptions of family and morality. Removing state recognition honors pluralism: religious communities and private organizations remain free to solemnize and bless unions according to their beliefs, but such ceremonies would carry spiritual and communal significance only—not automatic civil consequences. This shift prevents the state from privileging particular religious or cultural definitions of family and ensures neutrality toward moral diversity.

Contractual clarity and legal efficiency Private law already provides robust tools—contract, trusts, wills, powers of attorney, and property law—to accomplish practically every legal function currently bundled into marriage. Treating intimate partnerships as a matter of private contract encourages clarity and voluntariness. Parties could draft precisely the obligations and benefits they want: financial arrangements, caregiving responsibilities, powers of attorney, tenancy rights, and custodial agreements. Standardized contract templates would be widely available, and courts would enforce consensual terms while applying general doctrines against fraud, duress, or unconscionability. This is superior to the opaque, catch-all status of “spouse,” which often produces unpredictable outcomes and litigation over implied obligations.

Reducing state power, bureaucracy, and perverse incentives Marriage as a legal institution permits widespread administrative entanglement: marriage licenses, spousal benefits across tens of thousands of laws, tax filing status, family law proceedings, immigration sponsorship schemes, and more. Abolishing state marriage would simplify legal regimes and reduce bureaucratic overhead. It would also remove perverse incentives created by the current system: coercive or economically dependent marriages formed to secure immigration status, health benefits, or retirement payments; prolonged litigation aimed at preserving tax advantages; and social pressure to maintain a legally recognized union even when personal ties have dissolved. A contractual regime reorients incentives toward genuine consent and explicit agreement.

Protecting vulnerable people while respecting private autonomy A common objection is that abolishing state marriage would weaken protections for children, prevent mechanisms for spousal support, or leave vulnerable partners (often women) exposed. These are important concerns—but they do not justify preserving the institution in its current form. The state can and should retain robust laws protecting children, enforcing parental obligations, and penalizing abuse and exploitation. Parental rights and child welfare are distinct from a generalized marital status and should be governed by statutes and procedures focused on the welfare of minors, not on preserving spousal entitlements. Similarly, contractual defaults and statutory safety nets (such as equitable distribution principles applied to cohabitants who lack a written agreement, mandatory disclosure rules in domestic contracts, and targeted social assistance programs) can protect dependents and deter coercion. Where necessary, mandatory counseling, waiting periods, or impartial legal advice could be required before significant long-term commitments are contracted—much as consumer protection exists in other domains.

Addressing practical issues: inheritance, benefits, immigration, and decision-making Transitioning away from state marriage requires workable replacements for many practical functions. The sensible alternative is a legal architecture rooted in voluntary instruments and neutral dependency tests:

  • Inheritance: individuals can secure bequests through wills and trusts. For default protections, intestacy laws can be redesigned to favor children and close blood relatives; where people wish to benefit particular partners, they must state that intention in writing.

  • Benefits and public programs: governments should base benefits on demonstrable dependency, caregiving, or beneficiary designation, not on marital status. Retirement and health benefits should allow direct designations and administrative proof of economic interdependence.

  • Medical decision-making and end-of-life: powers of attorney and healthcare proxies provide clear, consent-based delegation. Statutory default proxies can be based on a prioritized list (e.g., legally recognized caregiver, parent, adult child), but these should be replaceable by explicit instruments.

  • Immigration and family reunification: family-based immigration can be reoriented around proven caregiving relationships and parental bonds rather than the marital label. Sponsorship should be based on demonstrable dependency or durable family ties, subject to fraud-prevention measures.

  • Name changes and ceremonial recognition: private name change procedures and community ceremonies satisfy cultural and personal needs without granting automatic legal privileges.

Rebutting conservative arguments about social stability and child welfare Supporters of state marriage often argue that the institution promotes stable families and better outcomes for children. Yet stability and child welfare derive from economic security, social supports, and accessible legal mechanisms to define parental responsibility—not from a singular marital category. By replacing marital privilege with robust contractual tools and neutral child-centered statutes, society can achieve greater fairness without coercing people into a legal mold that may not fit their lives. Furthermore, the state’s detachment from marriage would reduce the harms produced when legal recognition silences abuse (e.g., invoking spousal privilege) or when a marriage’s exclusivity denies recognition to nonmarital caregivers who actually perform essential functions.

Conclusion: A principled, practical shift Abolishing state recognition and regulation of marriage is more than a doctrinal change; it is a principled realignment of law with individual autonomy, equality, and pluralism. It eliminates a state-created hierarchy among intimate relationships, shifts bargaining to consensual contracts, and forces the law to confront real harms—abuse, child neglect, fraud—directly rather than masking them behind the umbrella term “marriage.” The transition requires careful statutory redesign to protect children and vulnerable persons and to establish default contractual doctrines and protections. But these are challenges of implementation, not reasons to preserve an institution whose legal privileges distort personal life and entrench inequality.

In short: the legal world should stop treating marriage as a unique status. Let families and communities define their own meanings and ceremonies. Let the law enforce agreements, protect the vulnerable, and secure the welfare of children. Remove the state’s special stamp from marital life, and restore to adults the freedom to arrange their intimate lives by consent, contract, and conviction.

Abolishing legal recognition of marriage means the state would stop treating “marriage” as a special legal status that automatically confers rights, duties, tax treatment, benefit eligibility, parental presumptions, and other legal consequences. Couples, families, and communities would still form relationships and observe religious or social ceremonies, but the law would not recognize a distinct marital category. Below are the central reasons and the commonly cited benefits of that approach, organized around the themes you asked for.

Respecting individual autonomy

  • Freedom of intimate association: Removing state-defined marriage frees people to form, structure, and end relationships without the government imposing one-size-fits-all categories or normative expectations about what a legitimate relationship must look like (duration, cohabitation, sexual exclusivity, gender composition, etc.).
  • Voluntary, contractual arrangements: Instead of default marital rules, individuals would use private contracts (cohabitation agreements, property agreements, parenting plans, powers of attorney, wills) to create the exact legal arrangements they prefer. This increases personal choice about which obligations and benefits to accept.
  • Decoupling civil rights from private status: Rights that should belong to people as individuals (healthcare access, anti-discrimination protection, privacy, bodily autonomy) are less likely to be gated behind marital status, protecting those who prefer not to enter into framed domestic institutions.
  • Dignity for diverse family forms: People in polyamorous, non-cohabiting, extended kin, and chosen-family arrangements avoid pressure to conform to the marital model in order to secure legal protections.

Reducing government overreach

  • Shrinking bureaucratic intrusion into private life: Abolishing legal marriage reduces the occasions where the state must measure, validate, or dissolve intimate relationships through licensing, registration, or divorce proceedings. That reduces administrative surveillance and control over personal relationships.
  • Eliminating state-sanctioned moral judgments: Laws that define who may “marry,” what counts as marriage, and what marital conduct is permitted become unnecessary. That removes a tool the state uses to enforce particular moral norms about sexuality, gender roles, or family structure.
  • Reduced incentives for paternalistic regulation: When marriage no longer confers automatic privileges, there is less reason for the state to micromanage domestic arrangements (e.g., dictating spousal support rules tied to marital roles) and fewer perverse incentives for people to enter marriages for legal expediency rather than genuine choice.
  • Fiscal simplification and neutrality: Tax, benefit, and regulatory systems would be redesigned around individuals and clearly defined contractual relationships rather than marital status, reducing the state’s role in distinguishing and privileging households.

Treating marriage as a private matter

  • Social and religious recognition remains private: Ceremonies, rites, and communal recognition would be matters for religious bodies, social networks, and the parties themselves, not for state licensing. Communities retain cultural freedom to define relationships as they wish.
  • Contractual legal architecture: The law would provide generic, neutral tools—property regimes, parental rights rules, fiduciary duties, default inheritance rules and protective presumptions for dependents—that individuals can adopt, opt into, or replace with contracts. These tools let people private-order their affairs while the state enforces voluntary agreements.
  • Privacy and reduced public registration: Without a state marriage registry, relationships and their terms remain more private unless parties choose to record agreements. That reduces state-collected data about intimate lives.
  • Market and civil-society solutions: Insurance, employers, landlords, and other private actors would adapt to respect contractual domestic arrangements (e.g., recognizing designated beneficiaries, cohabitation contracts, powers of attorney), creating decentralized, pluralistic recognition instead of a single legal status.

Additional practical benefits often asserted

  • Equality and non-discrimination: Eliminating a privileged status reduces opportunities for exclusionary laws; differences in marriage laws (past restrictions on interracial, same-sex marriage, etc.) would be less relevant if marital recognition were abolished.
  • Reduced “marriage for benefits” distortion: People sometimes enter or remain in marriages for legal/financial reasons (immigration, benefits, healthcare access). Privatizing these functions lets people secure necessary protections without adopting a state-recognized marital identity.
  • Lower state costs and litigation: Fewer marriage-specific registrations, divorce cases, and contested marital-status disputes could reduce administrative and judicial burdens.
  • Flexibility in family law: Law can focus on protecting vulnerable persons (children, dependents, domestic violence survivors) through neutral standards (best-interest tests, contract enforcement, mandatory safeguards) instead of entrenching marital presumptions that may be outdated or inequitable.

Caveats and typical institutional safeguards proposed alongside abolition

  • Default protections for dependents: To prevent harm to children and other dependents, states would retain child-protection laws, custody principles, child support frameworks, and presumptions about parentage based on clear, neutral criteria (biological parentage, adoption, formal parental designation), not marital status.
  • Preserving emergency access: Statutes can ensure hospitals, prisons, and officials recognize designated decision-makers (healthcare proxies, powers of attorney) even without marital status.
  • Standardized, accessible contract options: Governments or NGOs could provide standardized templates and low-cost registry options for common arrangements (property sharing, parenting agreements, beneficiary designation) so people without lawyers can secure protections.
  • Anti-exploitation rules: Contract law, consumer protections, and mandatory minimums (for example, in housing or child support) would guard against coercive or predatory agreements between unequal parties.
  • Transitional provisions: Policies would need to address existing marriages and legacy rights (pensions, benefits) in an equitable way during any move to abolished recognition.

Summary Abolishing legal recognition of marriage is argued to respect individual autonomy by letting people choose and shape intimate relationships without state-defined roles; to reduce government overreach by removing a major legal lever the state uses to regulate personal life; and to privatize marriage so social, religious, and contractual mechanisms—rather than government licensing—govern intimate associations. Proponents see these changes as increasing freedom, equality, privacy, and pluralism while shifting the law’s focus from endorsing a particular institution to protecting persons and dependents through neutral, contractual, and safety-focused legal tools.

Headline: In Praise of the Sacred Marriage License — Because Nothing Says Love Like a Government Stamp

It is a truth universally acknowledged (by at least one very loud subcommittee) that love, in its purest form, is incomplete until it is signed, notarized, and filed in triplicate. Indeed, without the state’s benevolent intervention, how would anyone ever know if two people truly love each other, or if they are merely cohabiting with suspiciously matching throw pillows?

To be fair, opponents of disentangling the state from the marriage industrial complex are not unreasonable. They simply prefer their romantic milestones to come with a side of bureaucracy, a sprinkle of legalese, and the warm glow of a municipal seal. After all, nothing says “forever” like a document that must be renewed whenever you move counties.

Let us consider, for example, the most common objection: “If we abolish state-recognized marriage, who will enforce the sanctity of matrimony?” An excellent question — right up until you notice that the same people who asked it also support inheritance laws, tax codes, and hospital visitation policies that seem to be working just fine without a ceremonial ribbon. The sanctity defense is, objectively, portable: it apparently travels well when carried in envelopes marked “estate planning.”

Then there is the “think of the children” argument, the rhetorical equivalent of a hug that smells faintly of Form 1040. Suddenly, complex social policy becomes a toddler’s problem. But the logic here is gloriously flexible: the children must be protected from the terrifying specter of unregistered love, unless the children need public schools, health care, or a playground. In those cases, the state is delighted to help — no license required, just a coupon code and a waiting list.

The tax incentive enthusiast offers another compelling line of reasoning. “Dual filing status,” they warn, “is the linchpin of fiscal stability.” This is the same argument that will, one shopping-trip later, be used to explain why two people living together deserve half off on pizza. It’s as if love and ledger are in a tango where one partner keeps stepping on the other’s deductions.

Some defenders of the current system prefer the sentimental approach: “Tradition!” they cry, as if the tradition were a beloved family recipe passed down through generations. Tradition is comforting until you check the recipe book and find that, historically, the book also includes footnotes like “wives must obey” and “dowry required.” But fear not: tradition can be modernized. We can keep the stamps and remove the shackles — or at least repaint them.

Hypocrisy, however, is the gentle seasoning that makes these arguments truly palatable. Consider the policy architect who insists marriage must be regulated because it is a “civic institution,” then votes in favor of letting corporations sign binding contracts with the same ease as a social-media terms-of-service click-through. If the market can certify a subsidiary with less paperwork than a marriage license, perhaps the problem is not love’s resilience but love’s paperwork.

Imagine a new reality show, Bureaucracy: Couples Edition. Contestants compete in challenges like “Complete the Affidavit of Mutual Consent” and “Navigate the Probate Gauntlet” while a panel of judges (wearing tasteful name tags) award points for notarized smiles and efficiency in filling out Schedule M (for Matrimony). The winner receives a commemorative stamp and a coupon for a modest reduction in capital gains tax. Ratings would be enormous.

Of course, the truly philosophical objection to removing the state from marriage is existential: without the state, what would people put on their wedding invitations? “Celebration of Love (No State Endorsement)” lacks a certain gravitas. But perhaps it gains another kind — the sort that doesn’t require a clerk’s validation to be real. Perhaps people might opt for private contracts addressing property, custody, and visitation — tailored, negotiable, and delightfully boring. Imagine couples negotiating prenups with the same zeal once reserved for choosing napkin colors. Romance, meet legal clarity.

The neatest trick of the current system is its ability to be both indispensable and optional, depending on the hour and the convenience. It is the Swiss Army knife of social institutions: a little bit sentimental, a little bit fiscal, and entirely fond of forms. Dismantling it would be messy. It might also be liberating. It would certainly provide an opportunity for new industries — celebrants with branding expertise, boutique contract attorneys, and municipal courthouses repurposed as artisanal coffee bars.

In the end, the debate is less about whether government should be in the marriage business and more about what we want marriage to mean. Do we want it to be a legal bundle of rights and responsibilities, a cultural ritual, or both? If the state chooses to cede its role, what remains is an invitation: to reimagine marriage as something people construct for themselves, with fewer stamps and more imagination. And if that makes some people clutch their clipboards and mutter about chaos, well — chaos once taught us the value of bridesmaids’ coordination teams and color-coded seating charts. We can survive.

After all, love has adapted to worse trends. It has weathered disco, avocado toast, and the era of unpredictable Wi-Fi. It will survive a world in which a marriage is as much a private contract as it is a public ceremony. And if not, at least we’ll have excellent paperwork to argue about in perpetuity.

    • Individuals would be free to redefine relationships on their own terms, without being categorized or policed by a government framework.

  • Reducing government overreach

    • The state would stop licensing, recognizing, or defining intimate relationships, and would not confer or withdraw benefits tied to marriage.
    • Public life would involve fewer official records and bureaucratic processes related to “family” status, reducing surveillance and data collection about private relationships.
    • Tax systems, immigration rules, spousal immunity, and other privileges or obligations tied to marriage would be eliminated or reframed as general rules that apply to all people, not a subset defined by marital status.
    • Government would intervene less in private life, potentially reducing moralizing or paternalistic interventions in how people structure their families.

  • Treating marriage as a private matter

    • Relationships would be treated as private covenants among individuals (and their chosen communities), not as public institutions or state-sanctioned categories.
    • Private contract law or civil agreement could govern property sharing, financial arrangements, parenting plans, and other interdependences, rather than a special “marriage” regime.
    • Religious, cultural, or secular communities could continue to recognize commitments and provide support outside of state recognition.
    • Public protections would be reoriented to apply to individuals regardless of relationship status, with obligations and rights arising from private agreements or universal laws rather than a marriage license.

  • Supposed benefits often cited by proponents

    • Greater personal freedom: people are free to choose how to form, end, or redefine commitments without government licensing or eligibility gates.
    • Privacy and dignity: intimate life becomes less publicly legible, reducing stigma or social pressure linked to marital status.
    • Simpler governance: fewer bureaucratic categories and forms related to family life, which could streamline administration and reduce state intrusion into private matters.
    • Pluralism and formal equality: since no one’s relationship is privileged by the state, the legal playing field is meant to be more neutral and non-discriminatory—assuming universal protections replace marriage-specific ones.

  • Important caveats and practical considerations (brief)

    • Protections now tied to marriage (survivor benefits, next-of-kin rights, spousal duties in certain contexts) would need replacement through universal or carefully targeted private-law mechanisms to avoid vulnerabilities for dependents, caregivers, and vulnerable adults.
    • Parenting, custody, and child support would need a robust framework that does not rely on marital status to determine rights and responsibilities.
    • Equality concerns: some argue that abolishing marriage could erase long-standing protections that, in practice, benefited certain groups; others argue a properly designed private-law or universal-rights framework could address these concerns. Either way, careful policy design would be essential to avoid new forms of inequity.
    • Cultural and religious diversity in how people choose to form commitments would be preserved but would operate outside a state-defined “marriage” category, which could require new norms, institutions, or private associations to provide recognition and support.

Title: The Ministry of Matrimony and Other Things Bureaucracy Beloved: A Satirical Guide to Opposing the Opponents of State-Free Love

In a land where love is illegal without paperwork, a brave band of truth-tellers has arisen: the people who still think the government should be the matchmaker, the referee, and the sponsor of every handshake and secret kiss. Gather round, fellow freedom-lovers, as we unveil the sacred commandments of the State-Recognized Marriage Preservation Society (SRMPS), and why anyone who disagrees with abolishing government involvement in marriage must be… well, wrong in many delightfully hypocritical ways.

Opening Scene: A Conference of Conflicted Contradictions Welcome to the annual “Let’s Keep the Government in the Love Business” convention, where the keynote speaker is a person who insists that “freedom” means “freedom to license your love but not to live without a receipt.” The crowd nods earnestly, holding up signs that read, I Love Tradition, Which Is Totally Defined by a Clerk’s Signature and a Fee Schedule.

The SRMPS believes, with all the gusto of a librarian at the end of a long shift, that the government should continue to license, regulate, and tax your romance for these essential reasons:

  1. Stability, They Say
  • Because nothing says stable like a legally mandated ceremony, a government witness, and a filing fee that rises faster than your excitement on the first date.
  • The argument goes: if two people can’t prove their devotion with a stack of bureaucratic forms, chaos—in the form of “economic uncertainty” and “emotional risk”—will ensue.
  • Satirical takeaway: If you’re worried about stability, perhaps you should also require a signed contract for cuddling on the couch and a notarized promise to share the remote control.
  1. Tradition (As Defined by a Rules Lawyer)
  • They claim tradition is endangered if “the government” stops overseeing who can wed whom, because tradition, apparently, is a spreadsheet with line items for each couple’s moral obligations.
  • Hypocrisy highlight: The tradition they defend is often a tradition that matches their current political wind, not the living, changing human story before them. In other words, tradition with a stamp and a receipt changes with the clerk’s mood more than your in-laws’ opinions.
  1. Religious Freedom, But with an asterisk the Size of a Postage Stamp
  • The argument runs: the state should protect people’s right to marry according to their faith, as if “freedom of religion” somehow requires the state to certify religious marriages and levies on them—though many religious communities already perform marriages without state compliance, and many who want state recognition don’t share the same faith at all.
  • Satirical note: If religious freedom is truly sacred, why outsource worship to the licensing department? Perhaps the SRMPS is just in love with the paperwork.
  1. The Kids, They Say
  • The legal frame keeps track of parenting rights, child support, and inheritance. The line goes: “If the state helps with legal things, it protects children.” The joke writes itself: a government office as matchmaker, guardian, and last creditor on the family budget.
  • Reality twist: If you’re truly concerned about children, you might want less state meddling, not more, so families can decide what’s best without a courtroom’s chorus of “We note your marriage, and we’ll judge your parenting accordingly.”
  1. The Market of Love (Price is Right)
  • They argue that the state’s involvement makes it easier to share benefits, tax breaks, and formal rights. The gag: “Nothing says ‘I love you’ like a tax deduction that could buy you a slightly more romantic toaster.”
  • In satire’s mirror: a system that promises equality through a fee schedule is, in effect, selling love with a receipt.

Mocking the Opponents’ Most Delicate Claims

  • Claim: “We’re defending families by keeping government in the marriage business.” Satire: If you’re defending families, maybe defend them from the complexity of a licensing regime that treats love like a house loan and couples’ feelings like collateral.

  • Claim: “We’re defending faith and tradition.” Satire: If tradition is the sacred shield, you’d think it would protect people from being taxed for something they didn’t consent to in the first place. But no—the shield is more like a receipt.

  • Claim: “We’re defending the safety net for kids.” Satire: A safety net is commendable; a safety net that requires a social security number, a ceremony, and an audit from a solemn clerk is… well, a safety plan designed by someone who thinks romance is a risk assessment.

  • Claim: “The state should regulate marriage to prevent fraud.” Satire: The best way to prevent fraud is… to regulate it with a license you need to buy, renew, and present to various officials, all while claiming to protect personal autonomy? The cognitive dissonance is delicious.

A Gallery of “Oppositional” Quotes, Reimagined

  • “Marriage is a sacred institution; it requires sacred paperwork.” Translation: Sacred paperwork is not sacred; it’s a vendor contract with a ceremonial badge.
  • “The state knows how to define marriage better than people themselves.” Translation: The state’s definition is a moving target, like a weather vane with a filing cabinet.
  • “If we lose government recognition, families will fall apart.” Translation: If you enforce marriage with a government card, you’re already treating love like a liability. Real families don’t need a stamp of approval to stay together; they need food, patience, and occasional humor.

The Great Hypocrisy Meter

  • The SRMPS preaches personal responsibility while demanding an entire bureaucracy to oversee who loves whom.
  • They champion freedom of conscience but insist that conscience must be logged, notarized, and subject to the state’s flavor-of-the-month interpretations.
  • They push for moral clarity yet rely on an ever-changing legal framework to decide what counts as “marriage” and who gets the tax credit for it.

Embracing the Real Two-Body Problem: Love, Not Licenses To the audience of anyone who’s ever paid a fee to make a life partnership “official”: you deserve a love that isn’t graded by the state’s ledger. You deserve the freedom to decide who you share your life with, and to do so without the government turning your romance into a consumer product. If you want stable companionship, you don’t need a bureaucrat with a stamp—you need trust, communication, and occasional vacations.

A Humble Concluding Manifesto (In Satire, For Real Reflection)

  • Let people marry whom they love, or not marry at all, as they choose—without requiring a government license, a tax form, or a ceremonious bureaucratic blessing.
  • Let families decide what works best for them: who steps in as co-parent, how to divide responsibilities, and how to navigate financial and emotional life—without a state-choreographer dictating every step.
  • Let religious communities perform their own rites if they wish, with or without civil recognition, while the state remains neutral, not the love referee of every private vow.

If you’re reading this as someone who values freedom, you’re probably chuckling at the idea that a democracy would equate love with paperwork. If you’re reading this as someone who defends the current system, please consider: would your love be happier, more secure, or more genuine if it didn’t have to pass through a government office before it could be recognized by those who matter most?

Final flourish: This piece is a satirical romp, not a decree. The point isn’t to crush all beliefs about marriage but to poke at the absurdities of insisting the state must own or oversee every romance. If you enjoy the humor, great; if you’re offended, also great—but perhaps that offense is a sign you’re thinking critically about how much of love’s magic we want to license.

Question:
Draft a passionate speech that strongly advocates for completely abolishing state recognition and regulation of marriage in order to protect personal freedom and remove government interference from private relationships.
Model Response:

Friends, fellow citizens, hear this call not as a whim but as a principle we owe to every person who loves freely and dreams of a life uncoerced by the state.

We stand at a crossroads in the deepest part of our lives as a society. We have long lived under a system that ties love to licenses, ceremonies to compliance, and affection to approval from a government that has no business meddling in the most intimate corners of our lives. It is time to remove the state’s hands from the bond between two people who wish to commit to one another. It is time to abolish state recognition and regulation of marriage altogether, so that personal freedom can breathe again and private relationships can flourish free from bureaucratic force.

Why should a couple’s love be surveilled, quantified, and taxed by the very institution that is supposed to protect liberty? Why should a government decide who is family or who deserves the rights that come with a lifelong commitment? Our answer must be this: love is a private covenant, a matter between individuals and the communities they choose to form. The state has no rightful claim to define the terms of that covenant, to grant or withdraw the privileges that flow from it, or to police who may share a home, raise a child, or stand by a partner in sickness and in joy. If we truly value freedom, we must remove the state’s verdict from the most intimate decisions we make.

Consider the heart of the argument. Personal freedom is not the absence of law; it is the absence of coercive law that claims to know what love must look like, or who qualifies as a family. The state’s fingerprints on marriage have, in practice, reduced human relationships to legal statuses and tax brackets. They have created a lattice of rules that incentivize conformity, penalize difference, and force people into categories that may not reflect their deepest commitments. When government recognizes a marriage, it also wields the power to grant privileges and to impose penalties. But if the power to love is to be truly free, it must be protected from government favoritism and government punishment alike.

We must face a basic truth: a healthy, stable society does not require the state to certify the legitimacy of love in order for people to form families, to raise children, or to build mutual support systems. Families have always formed in countless ways—across cultures, religions, and ideologies—without a central marriage certificate. They have thrived because they were anchored in voluntary commitments, mutual respect, shared responsibility, and a shared sense of duty to another person and to any children they choose to raise. If we are serious about protecting personal freedom, we should extend that principle to every kind of relationship, without the state's licensing or regulation.

What would replace the state’s role? Not chaos, but clear, voluntary, private arrangements. We can envision a society where:

  • Individuals freely enter into private agreements about companionship, finances, property, parenting, and caregiving—agreements that are binding by private consent, enforced by independent, non-governmental courts and arbitrators chosen by the parties themselves.

  • Private registries and contract frameworks help with matters that people typically rely on today (for example, wills, guardianship, succession, shared property) without the state labeling or privileging one form of relationship over another.

  • Civil society institutions—trusted religious communities, charitable associations, professional bodies, and neighborhood networks—provide norms, mediation, and support for relationships, while leaving the law of the land to general norms of voluntary cooperation rather than state coercion.

  • A neutral private arbitration system resolves disputes over contracts, parenting plans, asset division, and other essential matters with speed, fairness, and respect for the dignity of all parties, focusing on the welfare of any children and the autonomy of adults, not on enforcing a government-approved status.

  • Financial and legal protections are achieved through voluntary contracts that are honored by the market of private law, not by a government grant of privileges. If a couple or partners wish to protect each other, they do so through agreements they carefully negotiate—decisions they make, and then carry out together, with accountability to the people and institutions they themselves trust.

This is not a recipe for a cold, libertarian arbitrary order. It is a call to reconnect our social fabric to voluntary cooperation, to give families, individuals, and communities the freedom to craft their arrangements in the manner most consistent with their values. It is a rejection of the idea that the state should own the terms of love, sacrifice, and commitment. If we want to defend personal freedom, we must defend the right to pair up—or not—without whipping the relationship into a system that treats some unions as lawful, privileged, or protected, and others as insufficient, unworthy, or illegal.

Critics will raise practical questions. What about children? What about those who rely on the state for protections now tied to marriage? What about those who worry that without official recognition, rights would be uncertain or arbitrarily denied?

To these concerns, I offer this response: the welfare of children should be central, not used as a lever to preserve a governmental category. In a private-law, voluntary system, parental rights and responsibilities would be determined by binding agreements and the best interests of the child, assessed by private, independent mechanisms chosen by the parents and communities involved. The goal remains constant: to safeguard the well-being of children and to minimize coercion. We can establish robust, private guardianship networks, voluntary support arrangements, and community oversight that prioritizes the child’s welfare while avoiding state-imposed hierarchies of legitimacy and status.

And what about stability and predictability in a world without marriage licenses? The answer lies in voluntary, durable commitments and reliable private institutions that people can trust. People will still get married, if they wish; they simply will not be required to seek government endorsement. Those who want the social meaning of marriage can create it within their communities and through contracts that reflect their shared values. Those who prefer different forms of living together can do so without being penalized or privileged by the state. The market for private law, arbitration, and trust networks will respond to demand, create norms, and provide recourse when commitments are broken or misused—just as markets and communities do in every other realm of life.

Transition will require courage and a clear plan. This is not about tearing down protections or leaving people adrift. It is about reorienting our approach to freedom and responsibility:

  • We begin by separating civil recognition of relationships from the state, ending the legal incentives and penalties attached to marriage, so that couples choose only based on their genuine commitments, not on tax codes or spousal privileges.

  • We empower private institutions to handle rights and responsibilities through voluntary agreements, binding contracts, and private dispute resolution, while ensuring that protections for vulnerable people—children, the elderly, the physically or emotionally dependent—are maintained
